title: BASF Battery Materials focuses its portfolio on Cathode Active Materials - Batteries News
content:
BASF Battery Materials focuses its portfolio on Cathode Active Materials
Cathode Active Materials offer BASF highest potential for value creation
BASF signs agreement to sell its Battery Recycling business to cylib
BASF is taking the next step in the strategic development of its Battery Materials business in line with its “Winning Ways” strategy. The company will focus the division’s portfolio exclusively on Cathode Active Materials (CAM), where BASF sees the strongest potential for customer value, differentiation, and profitable development. Sharpening the portfolio around CAM builds on the strategic recalibration initiated in 2024 in response to changing conditions in the global electric vehicle and battery markets. Since then, BASF Battery Materials has adjusted its investment plans, strengthened its competitiveness, secured important customer agreements and started to evaluate strategic partnership options for activities outside its future portfolio.
Anup Kothari,
member of the Board of Executive Directors of BASF SE, said:
BASF Battery Materials operates in an attractive long-term growth market that is also characterized by significant market and technology risks,
“This next step in the strategic development of the business reflects the ‘Winning Ways’ strategic ambition: Enabling standalone businesses like BASF Battery Materials to compete successfully in their specific markets and maximize their value.”
BASF signs agreement to sell its Battery Recycling business to cylib
As part of its strategic focus on Cathode Active Materials, BASF has decided to divest its Battery Recycling business. On November 20, 2026, BASF and cylib signed an agreement under which cylib will acquire BASF’s Battery Recycling business. The transaction is intended to place the business in an environment where it can benefit from greater scale, complementary capabilities and closer integration along the recycling value chain.
The transaction comprises BASF’s Battery Recycling activities in Europe and North America, including intellectual property, customer contracts and partner relationships, as well as the Black Mass production plant and the battery recycling prototype plant in Schwarzheide, Germany. Existing customer and partner relationships will remain in place. Until the transaction closes, BASF will continue to manage the business and related communications.
Dr. Daniel Schönfelder,
President of BASF’s Battery Materials division, said:
Over the past several years, our recycling team has built competitive capabilities and industrial assets, as well as valuable customer and partner relationships
“With cylib, the business will be able to build on this solid foundation and benefit from cylib’s specialized recycling technology, growing industrial scale and integrated approach from battery processing to the recovery of valuable raw materials. The transaction provides a strong platform for the future development of the recycling business. And beyond, we look forward to shaping our industry in partnership with cylib.”
Dr. Gideon Schwich,
Co-CEO and Co-Founder of cylib, said:
With the acquisition of BASF’s battery recycling business, we are further expanding our role in the European market,
“Recycling is cylib’s core business. With Schwarzheide, we are expanding our network in Europe by another site where end-of-life batteries are processed into black mass. The teams of the business bring many years of experience and extensive know-how. Together with them, we will continue to build out our technology and the recycling value chain from end-of-life battery to raw material. This enables us to recover critical raw materials such as lithium, nickel and cobalt and to strengthen Europe’s security of supply.”
The transaction is expected to close between Q2 and Q3 2027, subject to approval by the relevant authorities and the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. The parties have agreed not to disclose the financial details of the transaction.
BASF pursues strategic options for sites in Battle Creek and Harjavalta
Furthermore, BASF’s Battery Materials division is pursuing strategic options for its production site in Battle Creek, Michigan, United States, and its Precursor Cathode Active Materials (PCAM) site in Harjavalta, Finland, both of which are currently mothballed. BASF is seeking suitable partners to build on the sites’ existing assets and capabilities.
Schönfelder
concluded:
Cathode Active Materials are a key differentiator for battery performance, safety, cost and sustainability.
”This is where BASF’s leading chemistry and technology expertise creates the greatest value for customers and where we will concentrate our portfolio and resources going forward. In recent years, we have secured important long-term customer agreements and reduced costs and capital expenditure. Looking ahead, we will build on our global production and research footprint, customer-specific product development and expertise in nickel-based Cathode Active Materials.”

title: ProLogium Presents Battery Pack 2.0 at NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop for Space Missions and Lunar Infrastructure - Batteries News
content:
ProLogium Presents Battery Pack 2.0 at NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop for Space Missions and Lunar Infrastructure
ProLogium’s GEN4 next generation battery is designed to strengthen mission resilience through intrinsic and active safety, high power with low heat generation, and dual sealing. At the workshop, ProLogium held in-depth technical discussions alongside experts from NASA, BAE Systems, Saft, The Aerospace Corporation and other government agencies on scaling the technology for space missions.
HUNTSVILLE, Ala., Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — ProLogium Technology made its first appearance at the 2026 NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop, where Founder, CEO and CTO Vincent Yang delivered a presentation titled “Mission-Ready Next Generation Battery: Safe. Powerful. Dense & Scalable.” Yang introduced ProLogium’s Battery Pack 2.0 design concept, outlining how its GEN4 Superfluidized All-Inorganic Solid-State Lithium Ceramic Battery combines high energy density, high-power performance with low heat generation, active safety mechanisms and dual sealing to address the demands of spacecraft and lunar infrastructure, where lightweight design, safety and mission resilience are critical. The official agenda featured technical contributions from NASA, BAE Systems, the Naval Surface Warfare Center, The Aerospace Corporation and Saft, among others. Building on its existing ground-test results, ProLogium aims to pursue flight validation for specific missions and progressively establish flight heritage, laying the groundwork for its expansion into the aerospace battery market.
Hosted by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center, the NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop brings together government, industry and research experts from around the world. The program covers advances in battery technology, flight and ground testing, on-orbit operations and fault response. ProLogium presented Battery Pack 2.0, showing how cell-level design can improve fault tolerance in space missions and support manufacturing at scale.
With Battery Pack 2.0, ProLogium is targeting two broad application areas: space mobility and infrastructure for lunar work bases. For satellites, spacecraft and planetary rovers, high energy density enables greater energy storage within strict weight and volume constraints, while low heat generation under high-power operation can reduce thermal management demands, creating opportunities to further reduce battery system weight. For lunar infrastructure, battery value centers on long-term reliability and power resilience. In the event of localized equipment failure, power systems must be able to isolate the fault, maintain power to critical loads and restore operation when conditions permit. The same scalable cell architecture can support different battery solutions tailored to the requirements of each mission type.
asked during his presentation. Battery Pack 2.0 incorporates fault tolerance at the cell level so that the cell itself provides part of the system’s protection,
When something goes wrong, how much of the mission can we preserve?
The cell’s own seals can provide an additional layer of protection if external structures are damaged. Low heat generation can ease cooling demands when thermal management capacity is limited. If a fault originates inside the cell, the built-in active safety mechanism can intervene before a chain of heat-generating reactions escalates. For mission operators, these features can help reduce the risk that a local fault interrupts the mission.
Aerospace Requirements as a Benchmark for Other Industries
Aerospace batteries must deliver high energy density and operate reliably in extreme environments, within tight weight limits and under strict safety requirements. These demands reflect challenges also facing next-generation high-performance batteries in AI data centers, robotics and critical infrastructure.
ProLogium sees the safety, reliability and system resilience required for aerospace applications as benchmarks for next-generation battery technology. If GEN4 next-generation batteries are validated under relevant mission conditions, the results could inform product development and commercialization across multiple industries.
Vincent Yang
, founder, CEO and CTO of ProLogium, said:
Aerospace missions push batteries to their limits, reinforcing the direction ProLogium has pursued for years.
” A next-generation battery must combine higher energy density with safety, performance and reliability. If a battery technology can meet the demands of a space mission, the advances it delivers could have a meaningful impact across other industries. That is the vision behind our GEN4 next-generation battery and Battery Pack 2.0. We are using the demands of aerospace missions to guide our validation work and open up applications across industries,”
Fourth-Generation Cell Safety, Power and Sealing
ProLogium’s GEN4 cells incorporate non-flammable inorganic electrolytes and heat-resistant ceramic separators to provide intrinsic safety, together with a built-in Active Safety Mechanism (ASM). Yang likened ASM to the battery’s “immune system.” Under abnormal conditions such as localized overheating or overcharging, ASM can stabilize the active materials in both electrodes, helping reduce oxygen release and heat generation and suppress the chain of heat-generating reactions.
According to ProLogium’s technical data, the ionic conductivity of its Superfluidized Inorganic Electrolyte (SFIE) is approximately five times that of the liquid electrolytes used in the comparison, while its lithium-ion transference number approaches the ideal value of 1, at which lithium ions carry all ionic current. Together, these properties can help reduce polarization and heat generation under high-current operation, supporting fast charging and high-power discharge. The Logithium cell architecture features dual sealing, combining an internal edge seal with an external aluminum-foil enclosure to enhance hermeticity and structural integrity for operation under vacuum conditions.
Ground Tests Inform Future Flight Validation
Two peer-reviewed studies published in 2020 by researchers at Kyushu Institute of Technology reported that early-generation ProLogium lithium ceramic batteries retained approximately 98% of their capacity after vacuum exposure and thermal-vacuum cycling, and approximately 95% after separate multi-axis vibration and shock testing. A 2025 study by researchers at Nihon University found that a rigid housing reduced vacuum-induced swelling in early-generation cells from approximately 19% to 0.065% under the study’s test conditions. These findings provide useful reference data for further design and testing. GEN4 cells and battery packs will still need to undergo flight qualification under the conditions of their intended missions.
Fourth-Generation Validation and Manufacturing Scale-Up
ProLogium has commercially shipped GEN 3.5 all-solid-state lithium ceramic batteries from its Giga-level manufacturing platform in Taiwan. Cumulative shipments across its battery generations have exceeded 2.4 million cells. Scaling production requires consistent quality management, strong manufacturing yields and cost viability. GEN4 cell material design does not rely on rare elements. Its streamlined manufacturing processes and reduced dry-room footprint help reduce the capital expenditure required for production scale-up.
At the battery-pack level, the cells’ low heat generation under high-power operation can simplify thermal management and reduce cooling system requirements. The cells’ dual-sealing architecture can also reduce reliance on additional hermetic sealing components, simplifying pack design and creating opportunities to reduce system weight and integration costs.
Building on its Giga-level manufacturing experience and scalable cell architecture, ProLogium will continue validating GEN4 technology, optimizing manufacturing processes and preparing for production scale-up. The company is also exploring high-value applications across aerospace, AI data centers, robotics and critical infrastructure, with the goal of translating its core battery technologies into commercial opportunities across multiple industries.

title: cylib signs agreement to acquire BASF’s battery recycling business - Batteries News
content:
cylib signs agreement to acquire BASF’s battery recycling business
cylib expands its position in European battery recycling and strengthens Europe’s security of supply for critical raw materials
The transaction comprises BASF’s battery recycling activities in Europe and North America as well as the black mass plant and the prototype plant in Schwarzheide, Germany
cylib gains access to the North American market and significant customer relationships in the US
Operations in Schwarzheide will continue; closing of the transaction is expected in the second or third quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals
Aachen, Germany, November 23, 2026
– cylib has signed an agreement to acquire BASF’s battery recycling business. With this step, the Aachen-based company further expands its position as a key player in European battery recycling and strengthens Europe’s security of supply for critical raw materials. Beyond the transaction, BASF and cylib will work together to shape the industry.
The transaction comprises BASF’s battery recycling activities in Europe and North America, including the related intellectual property as well as customer and partner contracts. It also includes the black mass production plant and the battery recycling prototype plant in Schwarzheide. Through the North American activities, cylib also gains access to the North American market and significant customer relationships in the US.
Dr. Gideon Schwich,
Co-CEO and co-founder of cylib, said:
With the acquisition of BASF’s battery recycling business, we are further expanding our role in the European market,
“For cylib, recycling is our core business. With Schwarzheide, we are adding another site to our European network where end-of-life batteries are processed into black mass. BASF’s battery recycling teams bring many years of experience and extensive know-how. Together with them, we will continue to expand our technology and our value chain from end-of-life battery to raw material. This will enable us to recover critical battery raw materials and strengthen Europe’s security of supply. We are pleased to have BASF at our side as a strong partner. Together, we want to drive battery recycling in Europe forward.”
Dr. Daniel Schönfelder,
President of BASF’s Battery Materials division, said:
Over the past several years, our recycling team has built competitive capabilities and industrial assets, as well as valuable customer and partner relationships,
“With cylib, the business will be able to build on this solid foundation and benefit from cylib’s specialized recycling technology, growing industrial scale and integrated approach from battery processing to the recovery of valuable raw materials. The transaction provides a strong platform for the future development of the recycling business. And beyond, we look forward to shaping our industry in partnership with cylib.”
‍A building block for Europe’s raw material security
Global competition for critical raw materials is intensifying. Battery recycling is a key building block for Europe’s raw material security. With cylib, BASF’s battery recycling business gains an owner for whom recycling is the core business, who brings complementary capabilities, and who will integrate the activities more closely into the recycling value chain. This will allow the business to benefit from economies of scale in the future.
‍The entire chain from end-of-life battery to raw material
cylib covers the entire chain from end-of-life battery to raw material. The company recovers critical materials such as lithium, graphite, nickel, cobalt, and manganese at a recovery rate of more than 90 percent – with a carbon footprint around 80 percent lower than in primary extraction. At its pilot plant in Aachen, cylib already masters the entire process chain. The OLiC technology and process know-how are now being transferred step by step to industrial-scale plants.
With the existing industrial plant in Schwarzheide, cylib expands its processing network in Europe, gains access to feedstock, and thus lays the foundation for gradually expanding its own value chain. Black mass is the intermediate product of processing from which the critical raw materials are recovered.
‍Shaping the value chain together
Operations in Schwarzheide will continue. cylib is coordinating the further development of the activities closely with policymakers and authorities at the federal, state, and regional levels. The employees of the business – in Schwarzheide and at other sites in Europe and North America – have extensive experience and know-how, on which cylib will build as it continues to grow. Existing customer and partner relationships will remain in place. Until the transaction closes, BASF will continue to manage the business and related communications.cylib continues its growth trajectory
The transaction is expected to close in the second or third quarter of 2027. It is subject to approval by the relevant authorities and the satisfaction of customary closing conditions. Until then, cylib will carefully prepare the integration of the business and will provide information on the next steps as soon as they have been determined – in close coordination with BASF and the relevant bodies.
At the same time
, cylib is consistently pursuing its growth course:
Our goal is a closed European loop in which critical raw materials such as lithium, graphite, and cobalt are processed and retained in Europe over the long term.
Dr. Lilian Schwich,
Co-CEO and co-founder of cylib, emphasized:
The agreement to acquire BASF’s battery recycling business is an important step on this path,
The parties have agreed not to disclose the financial details of the transaction.

Fortum Oyj – Battery Recycling reaches key milestone with battery-grade recycled nickel, cobalt and lithium materials produced in Harjavalta
Fortum Battery Recycling has reached a major milestone in its next-generation battery recycling technology by producing the first customer samples of battery-grade nickel sulphate, cobalt sulphate, and lithium hydroxide.
The samples produced during a pilot campaign in Harjavalta, Finland, demonstrate the technology’s potential to manufacture high-quality and low-emission battery materials.
Anssi Airas
, Head of Fortum Battery Recycling, explains:
Our ability to produce these battery-grade materials for our customers marks a major step forward in advancing battery recycling and strengthening regional supply in Europe.
”Building a competitive and resilient battery value chain requires not only additional capacity, but technologies that can provide a real competitive advantage. The successful production of these materials demonstrates the potential of our approach”,
The process is designed to produce high-purity materials from recycled batteries. A key innovation lies in the internal circulation of essential reagents, which dramatically reduces chemical consumption, minimizes waste generation, and further cuts CO₂ emissions. At its core, the process embodies industrial electrification, utilizing clean electricity to drive the transformation of materials without reliance on external chemical inputs.
Fortum Battery Recycling has a clear vision of a self-sufficient and sustainable European battery value chain, and the Harjavalta facility’s strategic importance is widely recognized. In 2025, the European Commission named it a Strategic Project under the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), and Business Finland granted the Harjavalta extension project EUR 86.4 million support. In addition, Fortum Battery Recycling has signed a grant agreement with CINEA for the project, securing up to EUR 40 million in funding from the EU Innovation Fund.
concludes,
Our recent progress demonstrates how battery recycling can help customers build more competitive and resilient supply chains while strengthening Europe’s battery materials ecosystem,

title: Giving lithium-ion batteries a second life: VoltR prepares to scale up remanufacturing - Batteries News
content:
Giving lithium-ion batteries a second life: VoltR prepares to scale up remanufacturing
With support from
Green Assist
, French company
is strengthening its industrial and financial foundations to scale up its battery-reconditioning activities, helping reduce electronic waste and demand for critical raw materials.
As Europe looks to make better use of its resources, extending the life of existing batteries is becoming an increasingly important part of the circular economy. French company VoltR is contributing to this effort by giving used lithium-ion batteries a second life.
The company recovers cells from non-automotive sources, including e-bikes, scooters, industrial and consumer electronics, and energy storage systems. These cells are then repurposed to manufacture batteries for industrial customers, extending their lifespan while reducing electronic waste and demand for newly extracted materials such as lithium, cobalt and nickel.
Having established proof of concept, VoltR reached a new stage in its development: scaling up production. Its €16 million investment project aims to increase the volume of used lithium-ion cells it can process and reintegrate into new batteries.
However, moving from a proven technology to industrial-scale production requires more than technical expertise. VoltR needed to strengthen its industrialisation strategy, address operational and regulatory challenges, and improve its financial performance monitoring.
This is where Green Assist stepped in.
Green Assist assigned an industrial-process expert for 50 days, focusing on two areas: industrial scale-up and financial performance management.
The first workstream involved an independent review of VoltR’s industrialisation plan, identifying technical, regulatory and operational risks relating to battery safety, supply chains, production flows and plant configuration. The assessment also covered production strategy, insurance requirements and preparations for ISO 9001 certification.
The second focused on improving financial and analytical tools. Green Assist helped develop a cost-accounting and reporting framework connecting production, sourcing and commercial data, alongside dashboards and key performance indicators to monitor costs, margins and operational performance.
A stronger foundation for growth
The advisory support has already delivered concrete improvements. VoltR’s industrial development plan was independently validated as viable, with recommendations for a continuous production line, stronger quality controls and improved battery-flow and storage arrangements.
The company’s information systems were also strengthened through automated inventory recording and unique batch-number traceability, allowing batteries to be Green Assisted from receipt through dismantling and testing.
This work has given VoltR a more structured industrial and financial framework for its next growth phase, while strengthening its investment readiness and providing additional reassurance to financial stakeholders.
The objective now is to turn this stronger foundation into industrial-scale production, giving more batteries a second life and supporting a more circular economy.
Maxime Bleskine-
CEO, GREEN ASSIST, said:
Scaling up battery remanufacturing requires more than proven technology.
Green Assist helped us challenge our industrial strategy, identify operational risks and strengthen our financial monitoring tools. This support has contributed to making our scale-up plan more robust and preparing Green Assist for its next stage of industrial growth.

title: From Europe for Europe: BASF starts battery materials supply to CATL - Batteries News
content:
BASF has started initial deliveries of high-performance Cathode Active Materials (CAM) from its production plant in Schwarzheide, Germany, to CATL, the global market leader in battery technology. In parallel, BASF is supplying CATL in its home market from BASF’s Battery Materials manufacturing plant in Changsha, China, demonstrating the company’s ability to serve customers in key battery markets around the world.
The deliveries build on the global framework agreement for CAM signed by BASF and CATL in July 2025. Since then, both companies have worked closely across functions and regions to advance the collaboration from product development to supply. Combining CATL’s leadership in battery technology with BASF’s battery materials expertise and local production footprint, the teams developed a CAM product tailored to CATL’s requirements and transferred it into production in Germany. This underlines BASF’s strategic focus on Cathode Active Materials and its commitment to successfully executing long-term customer agreements.
Dr. Daniel Schönfelder,
President of BASF’s Battery Materials division, said:
We are proud to work with CATL and to have reached this important next milestone together,
“These first deliveries are the result of close collaboration between our teams across development, qualification, production and supply. This achievement reflects the complementary strengths of CATL and BASF and our shared commitment to execution, speed and agility. This provides a solid foundation for our future collaboration and reinforces our confidence in the European battery industry.”

title: EU pushes back Tesla 'Full Self-Driving' vote meeting again, now set for December 15
content:
Tesla Autopilot
self-driving
Fred Lambert
| Nov 25 2026 - 7:45 am PT
The EU committee that could approve Tesla’s “Full Self-Driving,” now sold in Europe as Tesla Assisted Driving, across the whole bloc won’t meet on December 1 as planned. The meeting is now December 15.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed the new date to Reuters. The Technical Committee on Motor Vehicles (TCMV) has already discussed Tesla’s file at two meetings without putting it to a vote.
Another date moves
Two weeks isn’t much on its own. But it’s the latest in a long line of European dates that didn’t hold.
In late 2025, Tesla told owners the Dutch regulator RDW had “committed” to approving FSD in February 2026.
The RDW publicly corrected it
. The Dutch approval came on April 10. Tesla then pointed owners to an EU-wide vote on October 6, and
the TCMV agenda for that meeting had no vote on it
Even the new date took a minute to settle. Belgium’s Flanders transport ministry first said the meeting had moved to December 7 before the Commission clarified it’s December 15. Nobody has given a reason for the change.
And a meeting isn’t a vote. The committee can discuss the file again and push the decision into 2027. Elon Musk said on Tesla’s Q3 call in October that he’d be surprised if EU-wide approval took longer than the first quarter of 2027.
The math Tesla still needs
EU-wide approval needs at least 15 of the 27 member states, representing at least 65% of the EU’s population.
Twelve countries have recognized the Dutch approval so far: the Netherlands, Belgium, Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and, last week,
, where Tesla has started the rollout. Using Eurostat population figures, we count those 12 at roughly 29% of the EU’s population.
Germany is the obvious next yes. Berlin got Tesla to
drop the “Full Self-Driving” name in Europe
and then
cut the system’s speed margin from 50% to 10% over the limit
in exchange for its support. That would bring the yes camp to about 47%.
So Tesla still needs France, or both Spain and Poland, to get over 65%. Not a sure thing. Sweden asked the EU in June to reject the system unless Tesla removed the ability to drive above the posted limit at all.
There’s also a catch for owners. According to Reuters, an EU-level rejection would invalidate the national approvals already granted. If the vote fails, drivers in Italy, the Netherlands, and the 10 other countries who are paying for the system today could lose it.
Electrek’s Take
A two-week slip in a Brussels committee calendar isn’t too bad, but the delays are adding up. It’s December, the committee has other files, and nothing Reuters reported points to a problem specific to Tesla.
We also don’t think most owners realize what’s at stake. If this vote goes the wrong way, the national approvals go with it. Italian owners who just got the system would lose it a few weeks later.
What would help Tesla’s case more than a new name and a lower speed cap is data. The RDW still hasn’t published its test results, and Tesla has never released disengagement data in Europe or anywhere else. Governments on the fence, like Sweden, want to see evidence the system is safe, not a rebrand.
December 15 is the next date to watch. Does Tesla walk into that room with Germany, France, or Spain on board, or does this slide into 2027?

title: Volkswagen's new affordable electric SUV gets a sporty upgrade with GTI DNA
content:
Volkswagen
Peter Johnson
| Nov 25 2026 - 7:44 am PT
Volkswagen
gave its entry-level electric SUV a sporty makeover with GTI-inspired performance. The new ID. Cross R-Line tops the range with added power and style, but there’s more to it than meets the eye.
Volkswagen ID. Cross gets R-Line style and GTI power
The new Volkswagen ID. Cross R-Line is now
available to order
in Germany, starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.
While VW’s R-Line is typically just a style and equipment upgrade rather than a true performance upgrade, the range-topping ID. Cross version borrows its electric motor, battery, and chassis from the ID. Polo GTI.
The flagship ID. Cross R-Line model, which will go on sale in March 2027, will use the same 222 hp (166 kW) front-mounted electric motor with up to 290 Nm of torque, which VW said enables it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.9 seconds.
It will also use the same 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 266 miles (428 km).
The range-topping version comes with VW’s custom chassis technology, also used in the ID. Polo GTI, which includes an electronically controlled front differential lock, DCC adaptive chassis control, and progressive steering.
As such, the flagship R-Line model is 15 mm lower than the standard ID. Cross. The lower ride height and front differential lock help to improve traction, driving stability, and control, while DCC automatically adjusts to road conditions.
The 222 hp (166 kW) version debuts with an exclusive new Traction profile with different drive modes, including Eco, Comfort, Sport, and Individual.
While pre-sales for the flagship version will open in March 2027, the entry-level ID. Cross R-Line is now available to order in Germany starting at €37,225 (about $41,000), including VAT.
The entry-level version uses a 132 hp (99 kW) electric motor and a 37 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 195 miles (314 km).
The entry-level version gains “extensive” R-Line standard equipment, including R-Line style bumpers, vertical daytime headlights, and 19″ alloy wheels.
Other standard features include Volkswagen’s interactive ID. Light with LED matrix headlights, Keyless Access, Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC), and a rear-view camera.
Inside, all ID. Cross R-Line models feature sports comfort seats, R-Line trim, and progressive steering as standard. It also gains the Innovision Pro infotainment package with the “IDA” voice assistant.
Volkswagen has yet to reveal prices for the flagship ID. Cross R-Line with the 222 hp (166 kW) and 52 kWh battery, but it will likely be closer to €40,000 ($44,000) when it goes on sale next March. Volkswagen’s
ID. Polo GTI
electric hot hatch starts at €39,995.
The new R-Line trim comes after Volkswagen opened orders for the standard entry-level ID. Cross last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000).
What do you think of the new VW ID. Cross R-Line? Would you buy one in the US? Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the entry-level electric SUV to the US, but it will launch
the ID. Tiguan
in 2027, which will replace the ID.4 SUV.

title: NIO targets 10,000 battery swap stations and $52B in batteries by 2030
content:
battery swap
NIO Power
Fred Lambert
| Nov 25 2026 - 6:43 am PT
NIO says its energy arm, NIO Power, will operate more than 10,000 battery swap stations and manage over RMB 350 billion ($52 billion) worth of battery packs by 2030.
That’s more than double the swap network NIO runs in China today. And it comes from a company that already missed its last big swap station target.
NIO shared the targets today at NIO IN 2026, its annual technology event, held in Guangzhou to mark the company’s 12th anniversary. NIO Power also expects to deliver over 10 billion kWh of energy per year through charging and battery swapping by the end of the decade.
As of November 11, NIO had 4,252 battery swap stations in China, alongside 5,584 charging stations, according to the company’s latest network count.
Getting to 10,000 by 2030 means adding roughly 1,400 swap stations per year for four straight years. NIO added 679 in 2024 and 681 in 2025. So the new plan needs about double the company’s recent pace.
Even this year’s goal of “at least 1,000” new stations looks tight. NIO had 3,729 swap stations in February when it celebrated its 100 millionth swap, which means it has added just over 500 since then.
There’s also some history here. At its 2021 Power Day, NIO
committed to more than 4,000 battery swap stations worldwide by the end of 2025
, with about 1,000 of them outside China. By February 2026, it had about 3,700, almost all of them in China.
The energy target is just as aggressive. NIO’s swap network had delivered 5.28 billion kWh in total by February, after roughly eight years of operation. The 2030 goal is nearly twice that every year, although it also counts NIO’s charging stations.
Who pays for $52 billion in batteries?
NIO’s swap network is tied to its Battery-as-a-Service (BaaS) model, where customers can buy the car without the pack and rent the battery instead. That means someone has to own a massive fleet of packs, both in customers’ cars and sitting charged in stations. NIO says it wants to manage more than $52 billion of them in four years.
For context, NIO reported total revenue of about $4.7 billion in Q2 2026.
NIO has been moving the heavy capital off its own books. Under deals like its agreement with Zhongan Energy to build 500 swap stations within a year, partners own the stations while NIO handles the technology and operations. NIO Power says it has now co-built more than 900 swap stations with partners.
The hardware is also getting better. NIO opened its first fifth-generation swap stations in August, and they’re the first to serve all three of its brands. That includes the compact firefly, which couldn’t use older stations because of its shorter wheelbase.
NIO CFO Stanley Qu, who also heads NIO Power, presented the unit as NIO’s showcase for running a business with AI agents, using them to manage battery value, station operations, and energy efficiency.
The rest of NIO IN: self-driving, NOMI, and “AI-native”
The swap targets were only part of the event; everything else focused on NIO’s AI-fication.
NIO also launched NIO WorldModel (NWM) 3.0, the latest version of its driver-assist AI, which starts rolling out in December to vehicles with the Banyan, Cedar, Cedar S, and Coconut+ systems, pending regulatory clearance.
NIO says NWM 3.0 needs 40% fewer driver interventions than the previous version. It didn’t say how many interventions it started from, which makes the number hard to evaluate. It also claims a roughly 60% boost in drivers’ “sense of reassurance,” whatever that means.
The more concrete claims are about speed: NIO says overall vehicle control latency is down 54% and chassis control latency is down 78%, while training is five times more efficient.
NIO also unveiled NOMI Intelligence 4.0, a rebuild of its in-car assistant around an AI agent framework that can plan and carry out tasks on its own instead of following set commands. The first release, Cedar 2.0.0, will be filed in early December. Cars on Cedar S and Banyan should get it in Q2 2027, followed later by ONVO models.
Finally, CEO William Li pitched NIO as an “AI-native organization.” He argued the global auto industry is worth $7 to $9 trillion and that AI could add more than $1.2 trillion in value to it. NIO says it has deployed over 7,500 AI agents internally, with more than 2.9 million executions so far.
Electrek’s Take
NIO’s swap network is real, and it works. The company passed 130 million swaps this month, and nobody else has built anything close at this scale.
Tesla sort of tried battery swapping
and quietly dropped it. NIO kept going.
But 10,000 stations by 2030 requires a build pace NIO has never hit, and its last swap target slipped badly. So we’d treat that number as an ambition, not a forecast.
The $52 billion battery figure is the interesting part. It shows what NIO Power really is: a battery asset manager that also builds stations. That only works if partners keep putting up the capital and the batteries keep earning money over their lifetime. NIO has been
trying to get other automakers on board
for years, with limited results – though it appears to be starting to attract more players.
And the competition isn’t standing still. Chinese automakers like BYD are pushing megawatt-level charging that adds hundreds of kilometers of range in about the time it takes to swap a battery. If ultra-fast charging becomes common, NIO’s swap advantage gets a lot thinner.
Battery swapping is one way to recharge in minutes, but if you drive an EV, charging at home on solar power is still the cheapest way to fuel it. title: This miniature electric Bentley is ridiculously cool – and actually street legal
content:
microcar
Micah Toll
| Nov 25 2026 - 1:57 am PT
If you’ve ever looked at a classic 1929 Bentley Blower and thought, “That looks great, but could it be smaller, electric, and somehow still cost six figures?” then good news: your car has arrived.
Hedley Studios has completed the first 25 production Bentley Blower Jnrs, with the hand-built electric mini-cars now heading to customers. Deliveries are beginning in the UK before expanding across Europe.
The Blower Jnr is an
officially licensed collaboration
with Bentley, recreating the famous 1929 Bentley 4½ Liter Supercharged Team Car No. 2 at 85% scale. Unlike many scaled-down collector cars, though, this isn’t merely an expensive toy for cruising around your estate. It’s actually road legal.
In the UK and EU, the Blower Jnr is homologated as an L7e quadricycle, reaching over 50 mph (80 km/h) and offering a certified 75-mile (120 km) range. A separate US program is also planned, though it’s not clear exactly what classification the mini-EV would receive stateside.
Underneath the delightfully old-school bodywork is a decidedly newer 48V electric drivetrain producing 31 hp (23 kW). The electric motor sits across the rear axle, while batteries and power electronics are packaged underneath the car.
The carbon-fiber tub rides on a steel frame with leaf springs and period-style friction dampers, while Brembo disc brakes handle stopping duties up front.
There are some particularly fun details, too. The charging port is hidden inside a recreation of the original Bentley’s supercharger housing, while modern necessities like indicators, headlights, and even a reversing camera have been incorporated without ruining the 1929 aesthetic.
The first 25 cars are part of a nearly sold-out run of 99 First Editions. Another 250 configurable cars will follow, bringing total production to just 349 units.
And “Jnr” definitely doesn’t mean junior pricing. Configurable cars
start at £112,500
before taxes – roughly $148,000 at current exchange rates.
Then again, if you’re buying a hand-built miniature electric Bentley, value probably wasn’t the first thing on your mind.

title: Ireland approves 1,367 MW of solar in sixth renewables auction - pv magazine Global
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策 > 正外部性 > 可再生能源优惠 > 机制（电）价
政策分类依据: 爱尔兰RESS 6可再生能源拍卖以竞价支持电价批准光伏项目，属机制电价支持
content:
Markets & Policy
Ireland’s sixth onshore renewables auction (RESS 6) provisionally greenlit a total of 1,367 MW of solar across 22 projects, according to provisional results published by the grid operator. The weighted average offer price for PV was €0.10242 ($0.1121)/kWh.
Blathnaid O’Dea
25 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Residential
Utility-scale
Ireland’s grid operator EirGrid has published the provisional results of the sixth onshore Renewable Electricity Support Scheme auction (RESS 6). As in previous years, solar dominated this auction, with 1,367.24 MW of PV provisionally approved across 22 projects.
In comparison, just 188.05 MW of onshore wind was provisionally successful across six projects.
The weighted average offer price for PV was €0.10242 ($0.1121)/kWh.
On paper, RESS 6 results show an increase compared with the
860 MW provisionally approved
as part of RESS 5 in September 2025.
A total deemed energy quantity of 1,894.04 GWh was provisionally successful in RESS 6, with solar’s portion of this coming in at 1,317.48 GWh. Just under 1 TWh – 977.67 GWh – of solar was provisionally unsuccessful.
Four RESS 6 projects did not qualify in this year’s auction, all of which were solar. Thirteen projects withdrew – six solar and seven wind.
Most of the provisionally successful solar projects are in the east of the country, near where the country’s first utility-scale solar farm was switched on in 2022, in County Meath.
Irish developers Soleire Renewables and Harmony Solar were the most prolific developers by project capacity named.
Solar Ireland CEO Ronan Power pointed out that although the auction’s outcome was positive, more solar capacity could have been successful if the unsuccessful projects were included. Power said Ireland said effectively “said no to a further 1 GW of solar capacity”, turning down an opportunity to get more renewables on the grid.
But Power also emphasized that the results are still provisional and subject to final approval and implementation. “The priority now must be to turn provisional awards into renewable electricity projects on the ground. We should judge the outcome not only by the capacity awarded, but by the capacity that is ultimately built and connected. The longer-term success of the auction will depend on whether the projects awarded support can secure finance, connect to the grid and reach construction. We also need to understand what happened to the projects that were unsuccessful or withdrawn, particularly as the current framework places significant cost and risk on developers.”
RESS 6 results are due to be finalized on Dec. 9, with notice of awards scheduled for Jan. 11, 2027.
RESS 6 is the first RESS auction to implement the non-price criteria requirements set out under Article 26 of the European Union’s Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA). It introduced new pre-qualification requirements and non-price award criteria into the RESS 6 auction process, which
drew mixed reactions
Offers submitted in the RESS 6 auction were ranked using a Composite Evaluation Score (CES), comprising the Price Score, Resilience Score, and Energy System Integration Score. The ranking of offers weighed both price and applicable non-price criteria.
Ireland now has more than 3 GW of solar and is expected to surpass 3.3 GW of installed capacity by the end of the year, still short of its 2030 target of 8 GW of solar, as Power pointed out.
Most of the current capacity comes from grid-scale farms, but commercial and residential rooftop solar is also pulling its weight. This momentum is likely to remain following the government’s confirmation that it intends to retain its grant support schemes for rooftop installations into next year.

title: Italy awards 16 GWh of battery storage in second auction - pv magazine Global
政策分类路径: 政策 > 监管落实型政策
政策分类依据: 意大利MACSE储能容量采购拍卖为监管落实型机制，具体细分证据不足
content:
Markets & Policy
Italy’s second Electricity Storage Capacity Procurement Mechanism (MACSE) auction awarded all 16 GWh of capacity offered for delivery in 2029, with a weighted average price 12% below the level recorded in the previous auction.
Sergio Matalucci
25 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Italy’s second Electricity Storage Capacity Procurement Mechanism (MACSE) auction, for delivery in 2029, awarded all 16 GWh of capacity on offer across 16 battery energy storage system (BESS) projects, averaging 1 GWh each.
The results are detailed in the auction report published by Italian grid operator Terna. The outcome points to strong participation from market operators and greater price competition than expected. Initial industry reactions have been marked by disbelief, and a full analysis is not yet available. The results appear to indicate a highly competitive market, with awards concentrated among a smaller group of developers, creating challenges for projects that were not selected.
The auction, held on Nov. 24, 2026, recorded a weighted average award price of €11,382 ($12,450)/MWh-year. This was 12% below the €12,959/MWh-year recorded in the previous MACSE auction for delivery in 2028 and well below the reserve premium of €27,000/MWh-year.
Terna said around 67 GWh of new projects had qualified for the auction, while submitted bids totaled approximately 43 GWh – nearly three times the 16 GWh procurement requirement.
Projects representing the 27 GWh of submitted capacity that was not awarded now have fewer options. They can seek revenue in the merchant market, pursue tolling agreements or rely on Italy’s capacity market. A recent revision of capacity-market rating and derating coefficients will also affect projects in southern Italy. For a battery with a four-hour energy-to-power ratio, the capacity recognized for auction purposes, known as probabilistic available capacity (CDP), is 51% in the Center-South region and 21% in the South, Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia.
Regional results
The second MACSE auction confirms market interest in developing electrochemical energy storage in Italy. As renewable generation expands, flexible capacity is becoming increasingly important to the power system. The source also points to geopolitical tensions as a factor making electrification an increasingly necessary industrial choice.
The Center-South region recorded the lowest marginal and weighted average premiums, both at €10,716/MWh-year. The South and Calabria region recorded the highest, with a marginal premium of €12,792/MWh-year and a weighted average premium of €11,575/MWh-year.
The largest BESS project selected in the second MACSE auction was a 3,399 MWh installation in the South and Calabria region developed by Enel Produzione. Enel Produzione secured a total of 7,337 MWh, almost half of the overall capacity awarded. A2A Storage followed with 2,244 MWh, while A2A Energiefuture secured a further 364 MWh.
Other major awardees included BESS by Erry, with 1,667 MWh in the South and Calabria region, and Field Melfi, with 1,138 MWh in the same region. Other selected developers included ACL SPV 2, Five-E Italy Orange 2, Nardò Solar Energy, PVexo Apollo 2, Saturn and W Selargius.

title: UtmoLight, UNSW achieve 19.6% efficiency for 2.81 m² perovskite solar module - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
The reported result corresponds to a power output of around 551 W and represents a 15% relative efficiency increase over UtmoLight’s previous benchmark. The module was tested at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).
Vincent Shaw
25 Nov 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Chinese perovskite solar module manufacturer
UtmoLight
and researchers from the
University of New South Wales
(UNSW) in Australia have reportedly achieved a stabilized power conversion efficiency of 19.6% for a single-junction perovskite solar module measuring 2.81 m².
According to technical documentation seen by
pv magazine
, the result was obtained through maximum power point tracking (MPPT) tests conducted at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).
The reported full-area efficiency corresponds to a power output of approximately 551 W under standard test conditions.
The result represents an improvement of 2.56 percentage points over UtmoLight’s previous efficiency benchmark for modules of comparable size, equivalent to a relative efficiency increase of around 15%.
Maintaining high power conversion efficiencies while increasing module size remains one of the main challenges in the commercialization of perovskite photovoltaics. Large-area module fabrication requires precise control of thin-film uniformity, crystallization, defect passivation, electrical interconnections, and interface quality.
The collaboration combines UNSW’s expertise in materials science and device engineering with UtmoLight’s large-area processing and industrial manufacturing capabilities.
Earlier this year, the two partners
achieved a certified stabilized efficiency of 23.5%
for a 30 cm × 30 cm single-junction perovskite solar submodule with an aperture area of 676 cm².
The researchers eliminated the conventional nickel oxide layer through a fabrication process that enables the direct formation of a hole-selective contact.
The UNSW team subsequently announced plans to scale up the technology to a module area of 2.8 m², targeting a power conversion efficiency of between 18% and 19%.
UtmoLight has been working on the development of commercial-sized perovskite solar modules for several years. In November 2024, the company
unveiled a 450 W perovskite solar panel
with a power conversion efficiency of 16.1%, an area of 2.8 m², and a dual-glass design.
In February 2025, it
began production at its gigawatt-scale perovskite solar module factory
in Wuxi, in China’s Jiangsu province.
A month later, the manufacturer
achieved a stabilized full-area efficiency of 18.1%
for a 0.72 m² perovskite solar module with a power output of 130.5 W. The device was fabricated on the company’s 150 MW pilot production line, with the results confirmed by the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL).
In May 2025, TÜV Rheinland reportedly confirmed a stabilized power output of 480.5 W and a full-area efficiency of 17.04% for a 2.82 m² module developed by the Chinese manufacturer.
UtmoLight has also been working to improve the mechanical durability of its products. At the SNEC trade show in Shanghai in June 2026, the company
introduced two new perovskite solar modules
targeting different deployment scenarios.
Its 500 W Chuangshi S2 module measures 2.81 m² and features a dual-glass design incorporating 3.2 mm tempered glass. The panel passed front- and rear-side mechanical load tests of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively.
The company also unveiled the Chuangshi S1, a lightweight 0.72 m² perovskite solar module weighing 4 kg and designed for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) and rooftops with limited load-bearing capacity.
UtmoLight is targeting a power conversion efficiency of 20% in mass production.

title: Poweroad unveils modular LFP battery system with up to 245.76 kWh of storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Poweroad’s new battery storage system is available in high- and low-voltage configurations and features 5.12 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery modules based on CATL cells. The high-voltage version can also be equipped with a 20 kW electric vehicle charger.
Emiliano Bellini
25 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
The Meta Node battery
Chinese energy storage specialist Poweroad is showcasing a new modular battery energy storage system at the Genera trade show in Madrid, Spain.
Dubbed Meta Node, the system is designed for residential and small-scale commercial and industrial (C&I) applications and is available in both high- and low-voltage configurations.
“Both units are modular and can offer a storage capacity of around 60 kWh by stacking up to 12 battery modules,” Federico Larcher del Río, Poweroad’s country manager for Spain and Portugal, told
pv magazine
. “The towers can then be connected in parallel to achieve a total capacity of 245 kWh.”
The high-voltage system has an operating voltage range of 172.8 V to 688.8 V and a storage capacity ranging from 20.48 kWh to 61.44 kWh per tower. It features a maximum operating current of 100 A and a nominal operating current of 50 A.
The low-voltage version has an operating voltage range of 43.2 V to 57.6 V and a storage capacity ranging from 5.12 kWh to 61.44 kWh per tower. Its maximum operating current is 200 A.
Both systems utilize the same 5.12 kWh battery module, which relies on LFP cells supplied by Chinese battery manufacturer CATL. The module measures 590 mm x 390 mm x 133 mm and weighs 50 kg.
The manufacturer claims a lifespan of 8,000 cycles. The modules feature a balancing current of 5 A, IP55-rated protection, natural cooling and an operating temperature range of -20 C to 55 C with heating.
The systems support CAN, RS485, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth communications.
The high-voltage battery can also be equipped with an optional 20 kW DC electric vehicle (EV) charging module featuring a CCS2 connector and an output voltage range of 200 V to 500 V. The air-cooled device measures 590 mm x 390 mm x 215 mm and comes with a 3-meter charging cable.
Larcher said the product is being distributed across Europe and that the company is currently expanding its presence in the Spanish market through distributors such as AutoSolar.
“The system is scalable and very versatile when it comes to adding storage capacity,” he said. “If an installation was initially sized for a smaller storage capacity, it can be expanded in the future.”
Poweroad offers storage solutions for residential and C&I applications and is also expanding its activities in the utility-scale storage segment, according to Larcher.

title: UK small-scale battery deployment set to double annual record in 2026 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Deployment data from certification body MCS reveals small-scale battery storage installations in 2026 are close to doubling annual record set in 2026. Policy support expected to fuel further growth in 2027.
Matthew Lynas
25 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Energy Storage
UK small-scale battery storage deployment has accelerated in 2026, with the latest data from certification body MCS showing new monthly and annual records.
MCS recorded 73,115 certified battery storage installations to the end of October 2026, up from 41,460 certified installations in 2025.
MCS certification applies to battery storage installations with power output up to 50 kW. While not a legal requirement, certification is typically required by UK energy suppliers to gain access to payments for exporting to the grid.
Monthly certified installations peaked in July 2026 with 9,382 recorded. Nine of the top ten months on record for installations were in 2026, with 4,343 installations in October 2025 the tenth strongest month. Matching the installation rate from 2025 in the final quarter would see 2026 volumes more than double the previous annual deployment record.
The solar attachment rate for UK small-scale batteries was also high. MCS records show around 82% of certified battery storage systems installed in 2026 were also completed at the same time as solar panels.
Rising battery storage installations comes as the UK government rolls out further support for energy efficiency upgrades to homeowners. The recently launched Warm Homes Loan Scheme sees the UK government work with lenders to de-risk finance for energy efficient home upgrades, such as battery storage, to lower the interest rate offered to consumers at the point of sale. Means tested grants are also available for qualifying low-income homes.
More policy support is coming. Battery storage deployment is expected to benefit from new building regulations in England, which begin a phased rollout from March 2027. Under the new Future Homes Standard builders in England will need to meet more stringent energy efficiency standards, which battery storage and solar installations support.
Lisa Cooke, managing director of MCS, predicted that the new building regulations would support further growth for solar and energy storage deployment in UK homes.
“These numbers are only set to increase as the industry, particularly the new build market, prepares to deliver the Future Homes Standard. With this increased demand, the need for quality installations is more apparent than ever,” Cooke said, adding that MCS has redeveloped its installer scheme “putting quality at the heart of everything we do.”
The certification body is also developing a
product standard for battery storage.
Under the current certification regime, MCS certifies installation businesses and solar products, however it does not yet operate a battery storage product standard.
Solar products certified by MCS must meet a set of technical and safety criteria and requires third-party validation. A future product standard for battery storage could see manufacturers subject to third-party factory inspection and tighter cybersecurity rules. A consultation with industry stakeholders closed on Nov. 10, 2026, but an implementation timeline has not been set out – although MCS confirmed to
ESS News
that there will be a transition period for MCS certified installers until an “adequate number” of MCS certified products are available on the market.

title: Afore unveils all-in-one propane heat pump for residential applications - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
The new air-to-water heat pump series features nominal heating capacities ranging from 8.03 kW to 11.75 kW and coefficients of performance of up to 5.70. The systems can achieve an outlet water temperature of up to 75 C.
Emiliano Bellini
25 Nov 2026
Technology & Products
Heat pumps
Residential
Chinese inverter and energy storage system manufacturer Afore is expanding its product offering to include residential heating and cooling solutions, with the introduction of a new series of air-to-water heat pumps designed specifically for the European market.
The new products, which rely on R290 (propane) as the refrigerant, are intended for both standalone applications and integration into residential energy systems combining solar power generation, battery storage, and electric vehicle charging.
“The heat pump can be sold independently or as part of a complete system,” Afore Vice General Manager Dong Chen told
pv magazine
Chen explained that, through an external energy management system (EMS) featuring artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities, homeowners can optimize electricity consumption based on fluctuations in electricity prices while maximizing the use of solar power and stored energy.
The company offers both single-phase and three-phase heat pumps, with the latter primarily targeting the German market, Chen said.
The new all-in-one system combines an outdoor monobloc heat pump with an indoor hydraulic module integrating a buffer tank, a domestic hot water tank, circulation pumps, valves, expansion vessels, and an intelligent control system.
The series is available in three versions with nominal heating capacities of 8.03 kW, 9.88 kW, and 11.75 kW. Their maximum heating capacities at an outdoor temperature of 7 C and an outlet water temperature of 35 C are 12 kW, 14 kW, and 16 kW, respectively.
Under the same temperature conditions, the systems feature coefficients of performance (COPs) ranging from 4.42 to 5.70. At an outlet water temperature of 55 C, their COPs range from 3.08 to 4.06.
The three models have an energy efficiency rating of A+++ for space heating at 35 C and A++ at 55 C, as well as an A rating for domestic hot water production.
The heat pumps can operate at ambient temperatures ranging from -25 C to 43 C in heating mode and achieve a maximum outlet water temperature of 75 C.
All three outdoor units measure 1,257 mm x 440 mm x 892 mm and weigh between 112 kg and 126.5 kg. They feature Mitsubishi compressors, Shimge circulation pumps, full-DC inverter technology, and IPX4-rated protection.
Their sound pressure levels range from 36 dB(A) to 47 dB(A) at a distance of 1 m.
The indoor hydraulic module measures 597 mm x 620 mm x 2,110 mm and has a sound pressure level of 36 dB(A). The configuration keeps the refrigerant circuit outside the building, which, according to the manufacturer, improves safety and facilitates installation and maintenance.
The systems also feature a 7-inch touchscreen display, Wi-Fi connectivity, smart grid compatibility, intelligent load management, and a thermal disinfection function for domestic hot water.
Founded in 2010 and headquartered in Shanghai, Afore specializes in the development and production of PV inverters and energy storage systems. Its product portfolio includes single-phase and three-phase string inverters, hybrid inverters, low-voltage and high-voltage batteries, and all-in-one energy storage systems. The company has a commercial presence in Europe, Asia, Australia, and the Americas.

title: Belgium forecast to reach 28.6 GW of solar by 2035 - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
GlobalData expects Belgium’s solar capacity to more than double from 2025 levels, with distributed installations leading growth amid rising electricity demand and declining nuclear capacity.
Patrick Jowett
25 Nov 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Belgium is on track to deploy 28.6 GW of solar by 2035, according to analysis by GlobalData.
Solar is already the largest technology in Belgium’s capacity mix, the UK-based consultancy says, with 12.8 GW of installed capacity in 2025, equivalent to 43.4% of its total.
Attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, Power Analyst at GlobalData, told
pv magazine
he expects Belgium’s solar capacity to grow at a compound annual growth rate of around 8% to 2035.
He explained that as the country’s nuclear fleet contracts, falling to 2.1 GW last year, and with no new reactors committed to, most new supply has to come from renewables.
“Solar is the fastest and lowest-cost option to deploy at scale [while] electricity demand is set to rise as transport, heating and industry electrify,” he explained. “Electric vehicles, heat pumps and the industrial clusters around Antwerp and Ghent will all increase consumption.”
He added that regional policy, such as Flanders’ requirement for rooftop solar on large commercial and public buildings with high electricity use, also continues to support deployment.
Saibasan said the build out of solar will be led by distributed solar systems, which make up most of Belgium’s existing solar fleet, as land for large ground-mounted plants is limited.
“We expect commercial and industrial rooftops to be the strongest segment. The Flemish building mandate, high retail tariffs and corporate demand for on-site clean power all favour self-consumption,” Saibasan said. He added residential growth will continue but more slowly now that net metering has been withdrawn in the regions of Flanders and Wallonia.
Saibasan said grid capacity and revenue stand as the biggest obstacles that could prevent Belgium reaching the 28.6 GW projection.
“Distribution networks were not designed for large volumes of rooftop solar flowing back into the grid, so local congestion and connection delays could slow installations,” he said. “Frequent negative power prices at midday, already a feature of the Belgian market, also reduce the value of uncontrolled solar output and weaken the case for merchant projects.”
He added that Belgium’s federal-regional split adds complexity, with different support schemes, tariffs and permitting rules in each region.
“The most useful policy levers would be faster distribution grid reinforcement and tariffs that reward self-consumption and flexible demand. More consistent rules across the regions would also help,” Saibasan recommended. “Support for pairing solar with storage would let new capacity be absorbed without worsening midday surpluses.”
Saibasan told
pv magazine
battery storage is now the fastest-growing source of flexibility in Belgium.
He explained that grid-scale batteries are winning contracts in the country’s Capacity Remuneration Mechanism (CRM) auctions and earning revenue from [Belgian transmission system operator] Elia’s balancing markets and intraday price spreads. Earlier this month, Elia published the results of its
three latest CRM auctions
, with batteries accounting for a significant share of contracted capacity for 2028-29 and 2030-31.
Behind-the-meter batteries are growing in Belgium too, Saibasan added, citing the end of net metering as making storing and self-consuming solar more valuable.
Saibasan also said batteries will work alongside Belgium’s existing pumped-storage plants at Coo-Trois-Ponts and Plate-Taille, which have “long provided system flexibility”.
“Demand response, smart electric-vehicle charging and heat pumps will also play a growing role, as will Belgium’s strong interconnection with neighbouring markets,” he added. “In the longer term, electrolysis linked to the hydrogen strategy could absorb surplus renewable output.”

title: German agrivoltaics developer launches free tool for project planning - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Ylektra has introduced an online calculator to help farmers and project developers assess whether category II systems meet key agricultural requirements under DIN SPEC 91434, a German technical specification for agrivoltaics.
Petra Hannen
25 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Agrivoltaics
Commercial & industrial
German agrivoltaics project developer Ylektra has published a free online calculator to help users assess, at an early planning stage, whether category II agrivoltaic systems meet key agricultural requirements under DIN SPEC 91434.
The specification defines requirements for maintaining primary agricultural use at agrivoltaic installations. Category II covers low-mounted systems in which farming takes place between the module rows.
Users can enter the site location and crop type, along with system parameters such as row spacing, module height and orientation, and the working width of their agricultural machinery. The calculator covers systems with single-axis trackers and vertically installed bifacial modules. A traffic-light system assesses factors including land-use loss, cultivation access, light availability and expected agricultural yield.
Ylektra says the calculations draw on irradiation data from the European Commission’s Photovoltaic Geographical Information System (PVGIS), research findings from the agrivoltaic pilot plant in Heggelbach, near Lake Constance in Germany, and a meta-analysis by the University of Hohenheim covering 58 studies on the effects of shading.
The calculator does not replace detailed system planning or certification. Other requirements under DIN SPEC 91434, including water distribution, soil protection and decommissioning, must be assessed separately.
Ylektra recently published a freely accessible atlas of agrivoltaic projects in Germany. The atlas covers 2,697 projects in 109 countries.

title: Campaign aims to bring solar-plus-storage to 50,000 Indigenous homes - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Indigenized Energy says solar-plus-storage projects have helped families reduce monthly bills by hundreds of dollars as it launches a $2.5 billion fundraising effort to support a further 50,000 Indigenous homes.
Patrick Jowett
25 Nov 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Off Grid
Residential
Native-led non-profit Indigenized Energy and international advocacy organisation Global Citizen have kicked off a campaign to bring solar and battery storage to 50,000 homes in Indigenous communities across the U.S. and Canada.
The two organisations are partnering in an aim to raise $2.5 billion through philanthropy and impact investment to reach their target.
The money raised will go towards developing community-owned solar-plus-storage projects for Indigenous communities that often sit at the end of utility lines, face high costs and power outages that can last for days. It will also go towards developing workforce training and the local capacity required to sustain these systems once operational.
Serena Romero, Indigenized Energy’s Director of Marketing and Communications, told
pv magazine
the target of 50,000 homes is based on an estimated average investment of $50,000 per home.
“That includes solar panels and battery storage, plus, where needed, improvements such as appliance upgrades or other measures to make the home more energy efficient,” Romero said. “Actual costs will vary depending on the home, location, and scope of work.”
The number of communities to be the support by the initiative is not fixed, Romero added, but the initiative plans to expand Indigenized Energy’s reach into Canada through partnership with other Native organisations.
Projects are due to commence next year, Romero revealed, with installations in Pine Ridge, South Dakota, and with the Menominee Tribe in Wisconsin already planned.
“Construction in these locations slows during the winter because of cold weather and frozen ground,” she explained. “We use those months to secure funding, coordinate logistics and prepare with our Tribal partners for installations to resume as conditions allow in the spring.”
Romero added that the goal is to reach 50,000 homes over the next seven years, with the pace of installations dependent on funding and readiness in participating communities.
Indigenized Energy’s CEO Cody Two Bears commented that community-owned solar-plus-storage projects that are already operational have helped families see their monthly bills drop from hundreds of dollars to as little as $0.24.
Romero told
pv magazine
this example is one of several that the organisation hears of once installations are up and running.
“Homeowners consistently report bills dropping within the first few months and remaining low, sometimes reaching zero, depending on the home’s electricity needs and the size of the system,” she said. “Other homeowners who previously experienced frequent outages tell us they now sometimes do not even realise the surrounding community has lost power because their battery keeps their home running.”
Romero added that many of the households that benefit from Indigenized Energy’s solar-plus-storage solutions are part of communities that face significant poverty, with many living on fixed incomes.
“Reducing a $200 or $300 monthly electricity bill frees up money for groceries, healthcare, and other essentials,” Romero said. “In homes where multiple generations live together, those savings can support an entire extended family.”
pv magazine
previously spoke to Indigenized Energy in February about one of its
operational off-grid solar-plus-storage projects
in southeastern Montana.

title: OpenAI establishes exact 2.25 exponent for matrix multiplication
content: OpenAI researchers have published a mathematical result claiming to establish an exact 2.25 exponent for square matrix multiplication, potentially resolving a decades-old question in theoretical computer science.The November 24 preprint, titled The matrix multiplication exponent is nine fourths, establishes matching upper and lower bounds for the computational complexity of multiplying square matrices over every field, according to the researchers.The result marks a significant development in a mathematical problem that has challenged researchers since the 1960s. It also goes beyond an earlier OpenAI result published on October 2, which established an upper bound of 2.25 over complex numbers.The matrix multiplication exponent, represented by the Greek letter omega (ω), describes how the number of arithmetic operations required to multiply two square matrices grows as their dimensions increase.The conventional approach requires roughly (n^3) operations for two (n \times n) matrices. A lower exponent indicates that fewer operations are theoretically needed as matrix sizes grow.Matching bounds establish exponentThe latest paper claims that the exponent is exactly 9/4, or 2.25, over every field.Its central contribution is a matching lower bound for formal arithmetic circuits. The researchers state that, for every matrix dimension (n) of at least two, computing square matrix multiplication requires at least half of (n^{9/4}), rounded up, in nonscalar multiplication or division gates.The paper also establishes that the geometric border rank of the square matrix multiplication tensor is at least (n^{9/4}), while its asymptotic rank over the base field equals (n^{9/4}).These results provide a mathematical framework for determining the minimum computational resources required for the operation, rather than simply demonstrating a faster multiplication algorithm.The development builds on a long history of efforts to reduce matrix multiplication complexity. In 1969, mathematician Volker Strassen showed that multiplying two 2-by-2 matrices could be accomplished using seven multiplications instead of the conventional eight. His recursive method reduced the exponent from 3 to approximately 2.807.Subsequent research continued to push the theoretical upper bound lower, with OpenAI’s October paper establishing the 2.25 upper bound over complex numbers.Lean proofs support verificationThe November paper is accompanied by a Lean formalization, a machine-checkable mathematical proof framework designed to verify that formalized statements follow from their underlying assumptions.The formal development covers the square matrix multiplication exponent and related results, according to OpenAI’s accompanying documentation.A second paper on Euclidean geometry in the asymptotic spectrum of tensors supplies the geometric framework used for the new lower-bound result.The findings concern theoretical arithmetic complexity, counting mathematical operations rather than measuring execution time on physical processors. They do not establish that existing GPUs or computing systems can multiply matrices faster in practical applications.The result is presented as an OpenAI preprint and remains subject to scrutiny by the wider mathematical community. If its claims withstand independent examination, establishing the exact exponent would mark a major development in the study of computational complexity.
