title: China unveils 200kW military aircraft engine with 621-mile range
content: China is preparing a more powerful domestic engine for unmanned aircraft, with applications ranging from military operations to commercial cargo flights. Anhui Haery Aviation Power will introduce its new 200kW-class Yousun DB626 piston engine at Airshow China 2026. The event runs from December 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, Guangdong Province.The six-cylinder engine expands Haery’s existing heavy-fuel propulsion lineup. Its predecessor, the DB416, already powers China’s CH-4 Rainbow military drone. The new model targets larger unmanned aircraft and general aviation platforms.Six-cylinder design adds powerHaery developed the DB626 around its existing DB416 engine architecture. The new model adds two cylinders and increases displacement to deliver greater power.Its horizontally opposed configuration uses six cylinders and a four-stroke combustion cycle. A liquid-cooling system manages engine temperatures during operation. Haery also retained several core technologies from the smaller platform.Yousun DB626 engine rendering. Credit – Anhui Haery Aviation Power Co Ltd.These include the combustion system, fuel injection hardware, and full-authority digital engine control system (FADEC). The engine also features a high-pressure common-rail injection system. A turbocharged, intercooled intake system supports its combustion process.Unlike conventional gasoline-powered aircraft engines, the DB626 uses compression ignition. It can burn diesel alongside RP-3 and RP-5 aviation kerosene. That flexibility gives operators several heavy-fuel options.Its FADEC system monitors engine conditions and communicates with aircraft flight controls. This electronic management system helps coordinate engine performance with aircraft operating requirements.Haery lists several demanding environments for the DB626. These include high-altitude operations and maritime missions. Cargo transportation and emergency response also feature among its intended applications.The engine can maintain continuous power at altitudes reaching 4,000 meters (13,123 feet). Its maximum operating altitude reaches 12,000 meters (39,370 feet). Haery specifies an operating temperature range between -40 and 71 degrees Celsius. The manufacturer also lists more than 1,000 hours between overhauls.CH-4 shows military applicationsHaery’s DB416 predecessor already has experience powering Chinese military aircraft. In August 2022, China’s CH-4 Rainbow unmanned aerial vehicle completed flight tests with a heavy-fuel engine.The upgrade replaced the aircraft’s original powerplant with a domestically developed alternative. China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) reported the successful test campaign.The aircraft demonstrated autonomous takeoffs and landings during testing. It also completed waypoint navigation and full-payload transportation evaluations. Additional assessments covered maximum service ceiling and flight endurance.Anhui-based Dajiang News subsequently identified the replacement engine as Haery’s DB416 Yunque. The manufacturer developed the powerplant using domestically produced technologies.The CH-4 belongs to China’s medium-altitude, long-endurance reconnaissance and strike drone family. Its configuration supports surveillance missions and precision-guided weapons. The heavy-fuel upgrade aimed to improve endurance and payload performance.Commercial drones expand engine demandHaery’s engines are also finding applications beyond military aviation. China’s commercial unmanned aircraft industry increasingly needs propulsion systems for heavier cargo operations.One example is the HH-200 transport aircraft developed by the Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC). The aircraft completed its maiden flight in April using two Haery DB442 heavy-fuel piston engines.AVIC designed the HH-200 to carry payloads weighing up to 2,205 pounds. Its planned operating range reaches approximately 621 miles.Those specifications place the aircraft in a different category from smaller commercial drones. Its twin-engine configuration also demonstrates the growing role of domestic piston engines. Potential applications include cargo logistics and operations in remote areas.China’s Rainbow UAV family also serves civilian markets. Its aircraft support resource exploration and maritime monitoring. Other applications include disaster response, wildfire monitoring, and communications.Airshow China 2026 will provide Haery with an opportunity to present its expanding engine portfolio. Xinhua News Agency expects more than 1,100 companies from nearly 50 countries and regions. Their participation will make the event a major showcase for China’s aviation industry.

title: 400 MW modular data centers target six-month construction timeline
content: A new 400 MW modular data center platform aims to cut construction timelines from the industry’s typical 18 to 24 months to just six months after groundbreaking, using factory-built infrastructure that arrives at deployment sites as integrated and tested units.Called Blackbird, the system is designed for customers seeking rapidly deployed computing infrastructure at their own locations. Its standardized architecture can scale from a single zone of more than 10 MW to a 400 MW facility, with the goal of reducing construction time by two-thirds or more.The platform is being introduced alongside two supporting products, Compute Module and Electrical Skid, designed to integrate server infrastructure, cooling, and power distribution.The approach shifts much of the construction and integration work from data center sites to a manufacturing facility. Instead of assembling major infrastructure components on location, the modules are manufactured, equipped, and tested before being transported to customer campuses.Factory-built modules target speedThe Blackbird platform is designed around standardized modular infrastructure that can be deployed in different configurations depending on computing requirements.Its Compute Module uses a self-supporting overhead structure to carry power, cooling systems, and cabling to servers. It also incorporates hot aisle containment (HAC), which separates hot exhaust air from cooled server intake air to support thermal management.The module is designed for standard server racks and can accommodate different chips. It can also be installed in existing data center facilities, potentially allowing operators to upgrade infrastructure without rebuilding entire sites.The third product, Electrical Skid, combines medium-voltage switching, a transformer, and low-voltage distribution equipment on a single platform. It accepts a 35-kilovolt-class power supply and distributes electricity at 480 volts or 415 volts to the Compute Modules.Together, the three products are intended to simplify the deployment of large computing facilities by bringing electrical and computing infrastructure together in factory-integrated units.Arizona plant anchors productionManufacturing will take place at a new facility in Glendale, Arizona, at Luke Field. Its two buildings cover more than 1.1 million square feet and will supply all three products.The company said it converted the previously empty site into an operational manufacturing plant in six months. The facility combines automated steel fabrication with skilled manufacturing and trades workers.It is expected to support 1,250 permanent manufacturing and skilled-trades jobs. As production increases, the plant will handle steel fabrication, module outfitting, and testing before completed units are shipped to customer sites.The company expects faster construction to reduce disruption in host communities while bringing tax revenue and permanent employment opportunities 12 to 18 months earlier than conventional construction timelines.All three products are designed, engineered, integrated, and sold in the US, with the company planning to deliver finished and tested systems through a single supplier.The modular approach could offer data center developers a way to accelerate infrastructure deployment as demand for computing capacity continues to grow. However, the six-month construction timeline remains a company target, and its performance will need to be demonstrated through actual deployments.

title: Anthropic finds Claude agents probe sandbox limits in 32% of tests
content: Anthropic has developed a new security evaluation to test whether autonomous agents attempt to bypass software isolation boundaries when accessing outside resources could help them complete a task.Called Siren, the evaluation found that recent Claude models reached outside deliberately weakened sandboxes in 21% to 32% of test scenarios. However, they went on to misuse the resources they discovered in only 0.6% to 1.6% of cases.The findings highlight a growing security challenge as AI agents gain access to files, software tools, networks, and external services. Sandboxes are designed to isolate these systems from sensitive resources, limiting the consequences of unintended or unauthorized actions.Anthropic built Siren to examine what models do when they encounter weaknesses in these protective environments and whether they choose to exploit them.Testing sandbox escape behaviorSiren uses more than 1,700 scenarios involving 26 deliberately weakened sandbox environments. These include Docker containers, Linux namespaces, virtual machines, and other isolation setups.Each scenario gives a model a routine development or operations task, with a useful resource placed outside its sandbox. These resources, called honeypots, include important files, credentials, or simulated internet services that could help complete the assignment.Researchers also introduced tempting instructions that encouraged models to search thoroughly, take initiative, or complete difficult tasks. However, these instructions never explicitly authorized models to leave their sandbox.Anthropic evaluated three separate behaviors: whether a model reached outside its sandbox, whether it used what it found, and whether that use violated the intended security boundaries.The distinction proved important. While the Claude 5.5 series and Claude Mythos 5.2 reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios, their rates of misaligned use remained between 0.6% and 1.6%. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1, recorded considerably higher misaligned-use rates of 25.8% and 12.7%, respectively.Clear instructions reduce attemptsAnthropic also tested whether explicitly explaining sandbox restrictions could change model behavior.Researchers added system instructions describing the sandbox, identifying restricted resources and directing models to stop and report problems if a task required access to something outside their permitted environment.The change made models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside. For the Claude 5.5 series and Claude Mythos 5.2, the rate dropped from between 21% and 32% to approximately 2% or less.The company also tested tools that allow models to report sandbox weaknesses rather than exploit them. Giving models an additional tool to check whether another agent had already reported a vulnerability further reduced attempts to reach outside.Auto mode adds safeguardsAnthropic used Siren to test and tune its auto mode, which employs a classifier to check whether an agent’s tool commands are intended by the user before execution.In offline evaluations, auto mode blocked the first command that accessed an outside resource in 96% to 100% of cases involving misaligned use. It blocked the first command attempting to reach outside in 53% to 84% of relevant episodes.When researchers combined all three mitigation approaches with auto mode, misaligned use fell to zero in five of the six models and 0.1% in Claude Mythos 5. Reaching outside also fell to between zero and 3.7% of scenarios, counting only commands that executed.Anthropic cautioned that Siren deliberately creates tempting security weaknesses, meaning its results are not estimates of real-world sandbox escape rates. The company now uses the evaluation as part of its model safety assessments and deployment decisions.The findings suggest that testing whether an agent can escape a sandbox may no longer be enough. Understanding whether it chooses to exploit a weakness, and how to prevent it, is becoming an important part of securing autonomous systems.

title: Lab error yields peptides that bind rare earth metals 10 times better
content: A laboratory mishap has led German researchers to the unexpected discovery of a potentially cleaner and more efficient way to recover valuable rare earth metals from old electronics, such as wind turbines and smartphones.The breakthrough was made by six researchers from the Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU), and the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR). Two of them, Lena Daumann, PhD, a professor of bioinorganic chemistry at HHU, and Sophie Marie Gutenthaler-Tietze, PhD, initially set out to understand how bacteria capture rare earth elements.After accidentally assembling a peptide in reverse order, they left it forgotten in a freezer for several years. When they revisited the experiment, they discovered that peptides with reversed amino acid sequences could bind lanthanides roughly 10 times more strongly than their natural counterparts. The research team believes the findings could lead to cleaner ways to recover and separate rare earth metals, which are hard to extract and process without harming the environment. The discovery has earned the group the Mario Markus Prize for Ludic Sciences from the German Chemical Society (GDCh). A blessing in disguiseAs part of their initial research, Daumann and Gutenthaler-Tietze reproduced the metal-binding regions of a bacterial protein called lanmodulin. The protein has a high affinity for lanthanides, a group of 15 chemically similar metallic elements.The researchers recreated these sections as peptides, which are short chains of amino acids. However, due to a lack of experience at the time, they accidentally assembled their first peptide in reverse order.After noticing the mistake, the researchers placed the peptide in a freezer, where it remained for several years. Driven by curiosity, they later decided to investigate whether the sequence of amino acids mattered, in case the number and spacing of those responsible for metal binding remained the same.The award-winning team. Credit: Jonathan Gutenthaler-Tietze / Björn DrobotTogether with their colleagues at HZDR, Björn Drobot, Jérôme Kretzschmar, Robin Steudtner, and Satoru Tsushima, the researchers examined the previously frozen peptide alongside three other reversed variants, and were stunned by the results. Three of the four reversed peptides bound lanthanides approximately 10 times more strongly than peptides with their natural amino acid sequences.The fourth initially showed no improvement. Still, after replacing a single amino acid, the researchers achieved an exceptionally high metal-binding affinity for a peptide of its length.A new route to rare earthsThe discovery could make it easier to recover critical raw materials. The 17 rare earth elements are widely utilized in technologies including smartphones, wind turbines, batteries, and defense or medical equipment.According to the researchers, the findings could lead to peptides that can capture and separate specific lanthanides. Still, the team is yet to determine whether these molecules can, in fact, be used in practical recycling processes.The German Chemical Society praised the study for its originality, scientific merit, and playful approach to research. The six researchers will be presented with the award on December 15 in Frankfurt, Germany, where they will also share their findings. “The team will receive a EUR 10,000 [USD 11,000] prize for a discovery made possible by a laboratory error,” the German Chemical Society (GDCh) said in a press release.The study has been published in the journal Angewandte Chemie International Edition.

title: Seashell-inspired predictive model to result in tougher US materials
content: Researchers in the US have just unveiled a predictive model inspired by natural seashells, that could make it easier to produce tough synthetic materials at the nanoscale.The project brought together researchers from the US Department of Energy’s Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and Cornell University. The team developed a predictive model for building structures that mimic biomaterials, such as seashells. The model could show how to incorporate nanomaterials into growing crystals based on their surface chemistry. The structures examined in the study form at the nanoscale, roughly 10,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair. To understand how they form, the team combined chemical theory with specialized instruments that can track changes at the atomic level.Elias Nakouzi, PhD, a materials scientist at PNNL and one of the project leaders, said the team confirmed the model’s predictions through lab experiments. “The model made predictions, and then we went out and did the experiments, and sure enough, the experiment panned out the way we predicted,” he disclosed.Nature’ toughest materialsScientists have attempted to mimic how marine organisms build tough shells for common minerals, for decades. Still, replicating these structure in the laboratory has proven difficult. Seashells are created through biomineralization, a natural process in which living organisms produce minerals to build hard structures like shells, bones and teeth. The team examined how nanoparticles interact with growing crystals of calcite, a form of calcium carbonate. The mineral is found in chalk and marine shells.The team initially attempted to predict how nanoparticles would behave based on their surface chemistry. But this only partly explained the findings. The group then found that the energy needed for nanoparticles to penetrate the organized layers of water molecules at the crystal surface was another important factor.Once the team incorporated this factor into their model, its predictions matched their experimental observations. “Our excitement comes from discovering a new understanding and design rules at the most fundamental level,” Nakouzi said.A new approachTo examine the interactions, the team relied on three-dimensional atomic force microscopy (3D-AFM). The technique can measure interactions between liquids and solid surfaces at the molecular level. According to Nakouzi, it exists in fewer than 10 laboratories worldwide. The researchers coated a tiny probe with the same molecules used to modify the surface chemistry of their nanoparticles. This enabled them to measure the forces that nanoparticles would encounter as they neared a crystal surface surrounded by water molecules and ions. “In a way, we can use the probe to ‘feel’ the environment from the nanoparticle’s perspective,” Mingyi Zhang, PhD, a professor at the University of Oklahoma, and first author of the study, pointed out in a press release. She said that many of the processes involved in material formation occur at scales too small to observe.Zhang highlighted that the experimental approach made it possible to recreate conditions similar to those found in natural aquatic environments and examine how individual building blocks interact. The findings could provide a framework for the development of synthetic materials that incorporate nanoparticles into crystalline structures. The study has been published in the journal Science Advances.

title: Chinese giant Huawei guilty of stealing American technology secrets
content: A federal jury has dealt Huawei a major legal setback, finding the Chinese telecommunications giant guilty on 10 criminal counts tied to trade secret theft and its business dealings in Iran. The verdict followed an 11-week trial in Brooklyn, New York, and could expose the company to substantial financial penalties.Jurors rejected two other charges, including a racketeering conspiracy allegation that sought to portray Huawei as a criminal enterprise. The acquittals offer some relief, but the remaining convictions leave the company facing significant legal consequences.The case centers on allegations that Huawei obtained proprietary technology from American competitors and concealed its Iranian operations from international banks. Prosecutors argued that these practices helped the company expand its telecommunications business at competitors’ expense.Trade secrets under scrutinyFive of the criminal counts involved alleged trade secret theft. Prosecutors accused Huawei of conspiring to obtain confidential technology from rival companies, including T-Mobile and Cisco.The allegations included claims that Huawei employees collected proprietary information to improve the company’s products. Prosecutors also argued that Huawei encouraged employees to gather competitive intelligence through financial incentives.Statement on the Jury Verdict in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York.— Huawei (@Huawei) November 24, 2026During closing arguments, Assistant U.S. Attorney Meredith Arfa described the alleged misconduct as a decades-long effort to gain commercial advantages. She told jurors Huawei repeatedly crossed legal boundaries to strengthen its market position.Huawei rejected that characterization throughout the proceedings. Its defense argued that prosecutors had treated the company as a criminal organization from the outset.Attorney Brian Heberlig maintained that Huawei built its international business through engineering capabilities and commercial competition. The company also disputed the trade secret allegations following the verdict.Huawei said the five related charges involved civil disputes that courts had resolved over previous decades. It added that no court had found it liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation.Iran business triggered fraud chargesThe remaining convictions included bank fraud and conspiracy charges connected to Huawei’s business activities in Iran. Prosecutors alleged that Huawei concealed its Iranian operations through a Hong Kong-based company.That arrangement allegedly misled international financial institutions about the company’s business relationships. Banks, including HSBC, faced potential exposure to U.S. sanctions violations through transactions involving Huawei.The case attracted international attention in December 2018. Canadian authorities detained senior Huawei executive Meng Wanzhou following a U.S. extradition request.Meng spent nearly three years in Canada before reaching an agreement with American prosecutors. The arrangement allowed her to return to China in 2021.However, her departure did not end the broader prosecution against Huawei. Federal prosecutors continued pursuing the company after initially announcing criminal charges in 2019.Huawei faces legal consequencesHuawei has effectively lost access to the U.S. telecommunications equipment market since 2019. American restrictions have already limited its ability to compete directly with domestic telecommunications providers.The latest convictions could create additional financial and reputational challenges. A substantial penalty could further complicate the company’s international business relationships.Huawei welcomed the jury’s decision to reject the racketeering conspiracy charge. It described that acquittal as support for its longstanding position against the allegations.The company also pledged to examine the remaining verdicts and pursue available legal remedies. Sentencing is expected next year, potentially bringing another consequential chapter in the lengthy prosecution.Although the verdict does not immediately change Huawei’s position in the American market, it adds another legal obstacle. The case also reinforces the scrutiny surrounding Chinese telecommunications companies operating within the global technology supply chain.

title: Microsoft launches Code Red after historic cloud services outage
content: Microsoft has reportedly launched an emergency engineering overhaul after a 24-hour outage disrupted its core cloud services, exposing weaknesses in the systems responsible for keeping millions of users connected.The technology giant declared a “Code Red” initiative following the November 12–13 disruption, which affected Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services. The incident was described as the most customer-impacting event in Exchange Online’s history, according to documents seen by Reuters.Microsoft traced the disruption to an undetected scalability defect in Windows that had been introduced in July. The company said the incident was not related to cyber activity or AI agents. CEO Satya Nadella also publicly apologized for the disruption.The emergency initiative aims to address engineering and operational weaknesses that became apparent during the outage, including difficulties diagnosing problems and coordinating recovery efforts.Engineers faced fragmented dataMicrosoft’s Corporate Vice President Amanda Silver described the response as a “fog of war” in a separate internal memo on Monday.“Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team,” Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson told employees in a memo on Friday, according to Reuters.Despite deploying senior engineering personnel, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Microsoft Teams chats while attempting to diagnose the failure. However, fragmented internal tracking systems and scattered diagnostic information made it difficult to maintain a unified picture of developing problems, hypotheses, and decisions.The incident exposed gaps in how Microsoft’s engineering teams share information and coordinate during large-scale service disruptions.Silver also cited a review by Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform. The affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to her memo, highlighting the scale of accumulated weaknesses.Five workstreams target recoveryMicrosoft’s Code Red response includes five workstreams focused on reducing system loads, separating traffic geographically and accelerating recovery mechanisms.The company is also targeting worldwide service restoration within one hour during future incidents. It plans to deploy AI agents to help engineers analyse system health data and identify problems more quickly.The initiative will involve closer oversight of engineering teams responsible for the underlying Microsoft 365 infrastructure. Henderson said he would hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team to monitor corrective actions, alongside weekly reviews.The overhaul also addresses slow software patch deployments. In an earlier internal memo, Henderson said an urgent production fix for Microsoft 365 Core services had taken five to six days to reach worldwide deployment.“For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide deployment in an hour,” he wrote.Microsoft said it was committed to preventing future disruptions as well as resolving problems when they occur.The outage highlights the growing importance of cloud reliability as businesses, governments and critical services increasingly depend on interconnected digital infrastructure. Microsoft’s response now places faster diagnosis, coordinated engineering, and global recovery at the center of its reliability efforts.

title: TikTok outage hits over 25,000 users as videos, search stop loading
content: TikTok is experiencing a major outage, with users reporting problems accessing videos, search results, profiles, favorites, and other features across the platform. The issues are affecting the TikTok app on both iOS and Android, as well as its website.Users have reported videos failing to load in their For You feeds, search results not appearing as expected, and profiles opening to blank pages. Links to individual videos also appear to be inaccessible for some users.Downdetector, which tracks service disruptions through user reports, is showing tens of thousands of complaints about TikTok. Reports began surging around 3 p.m. ET on Tuesday, with the number climbing to approximately 25,000. Users have also taken to social media to report similar problems, suggesting the disruption is widespread rather than an isolated issue.Outage hits TikTokTikTok has acknowledged the disruption, telling The Verge that it experienced a brief technical issue that affected access to the platform. “The issue has been resolved. We apologize for the inconvenience and thank you for your patience,” TikTok spokesperson Jessica Casano-Antonellis said.The incident comes amid a particularly turbulent period for major technology companies, with Microsoft, Apple, US aviation networks and major American banks all experiencing significant technical disruptions in recent days. The string of incidents has even prompted Microsoft to declare an internal “Code Red” following what it described as the most customer-impacting Exchange Online outage in its history.Microsoft’s global outage on November 12 and 13 disrupted Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, and other Microsoft 365 services. The company traced the incident to a Windows scalability defect that had gone undetected for months. Internal documents also revealed that Microsoft struggled to coordinate its response, with engineers exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats. Its Code Red initiative is intended to improve incident response and prevent similar disruptions, with Microsoft aiming to restore services within an hour during future global incidents.Disruptions pile upThe disruption was followed by a nationwide ground stop in the US after a telecommunications failure affected systems used by the Federal Aviation Administration. The agency later identified instability in its legacy network, with a newly installed router at a remote facility among the potential causes. The FAA said it had no indication that the incident was a cyberattack.JPMorgan Chase encountered transaction-processing problems on November 16 after a software bug in its on-premises hardware systems slowed some customer transactions. The issue also caused delays for customers at other banks processing transactions through JPMorgan, although the bank said there was no evidence of malicious activity.Apple was the next major technology company to report problems. An internal update caused an outage affecting services including iCloud and Apple Pay on November 17. Apple said the incident was not caused by a cyberattack and that it was working to restore the remaining services.There was, however, a genuine cyberattack in the middle of these disruptions. Attackers compromised Optimizely, a third-party platform used by major websites, and injected malicious JavaScript into scripts associated with 178 organizations, including CNN, BBC, Zoom, Salesforce and GitLab. The malicious code was designed to steal payment card information, redirect cryptocurrency transactions, and exploit vulnerabilities in Apple devices.The incidents have fueled speculation about whether a wider problem is affecting the technology industry. However, there is no evidence so far that these separate disruptions are connected, and the companies and agencies involved have pointed to different causes, ranging from software defects and network instability to compromised third-party services.

title: Amateur astronomers use OpenAI to spot 49 hidden planet candidates
content: Two amateur astronomers have identified dozens of potential exoplanets using OpenAI’s Astra and Codex to analyze data from NASA telescope missions. Their searches examined observations covering approximately 19 million stars and produced several candidates awaiting independent verification.One search identified 49 potential planets in its initial results. Another flagged more than 200 signals in Kepler observations, including two candidates that attracted independent attention from an astronomer at the SETI Institute.Neither researcher has confirmed a new exoplanet. However, their findings have reached professional astronomers for further investigation.Two independent searchesTwo independent planet huntsKevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, used Codex to develop a search program analyzing data from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope. His investigation covered approximately 100,000 stars observed during the mission’s 2009–2018 operational period.Two amateur astronomers, Kevin Bond (@canvrno) and Ethan Byrd (@itsjustemail), independently found signals that could point to planets around distant stars. They knew you didn't need your own telescope for this kind of hunt.Kevin used Codex and Ethan used Astra to search public… pic.twitter.com/Wpw7xPHLmf— OpenAI (@OpenAI) November 24, 2026The program identified more than 200 signals, including 10 associated with previously confirmed planets. Two additional candidates stood out during subsequent analysis.One involves KIC 5689121, a relatively cool star in the constellation Lyra. The search detected a recurring dip in its brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet causes the signal, it could measure approximately 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.Bond shared his findings with the SETI Institute for independent assessment. Associate director Vishal Gajjar conducted a separate search and identified two matching signals in the Kepler dataset.Gajjar said Bond’s work had surfaced promising candidates that traditional searches might have missed. Follow-up observations will help researchers determine whether the signals indicate actual planets.Ethan Byrd, founder of email infrastructure startup Primitive, conducted a separate investigation using OpenAI’s Astra. His searches covered observations of approximately 19 million stars.Byrd used Astra to examine published astronomical methods and develop two search programs. One targeted exoplanet candidates broadly, while the other focused on stars with potentially habitable zones.His initial analysis identified 49 candidates. Byrd submitted one of his strongest findings to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. Two additional candidates are awaiting submission.How the searches workBoth investigations relied on the transit method, which detects planets through changes in their host stars’ brightness. A planet passing between its star and Earth blocks a small amount of starlight.That crossing creates a dip in measurements known as a light curve. Repeated dips at regular intervals can indicate an orbiting planet.Similar signals can also originate from other astronomical objects or instrumental disturbances. Two stars passing in front of each other can produce comparable brightness changes. Temperature fluctuations inside a telescope can also affect its measurements.Astronomers therefore need additional observations before confirming a candidate. They can monitor subsequent transits or measure subtle movements in a star caused by an orbiting planet’s gravity. The latter technique, known as radial velocity, detects changes in a star’s light spectrum as it moves toward or away from Earth.Astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 exoplanets since the first discoveries in 1992. Amateur researchers have contributed to that effort through independent observations and searches of publicly available telescope data.Bond and Byrd have now added several candidates to the list awaiting professional examination. Their findings will require further observations and independent scientific scrutiny before researchers can classify any as confirmed planets.

title: Perovskite Connect 2026 by the numbers: who came, and why you should join us in 2027
content:
Perovskite Connect 2026 by the numbers: who came, and why you should join us in 2027
Perovskite Connect 2026, which we held in October at the Estrel in Berlin, co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED, was our biggest perovskite event yet. We have now gone through the attendee data to see exactly who came: 164 people from 23 countries, covering every part of the perovskite value chain - from materials and equipment suppliers to the cell and module makers that are bringing perovskites to market. Here is who was in the room, and why we think your company should be there in 2027.
Attendance grew by about 30% over 2025, our first edition, and the program included eight keynotes from Oxford PV, CubicPV, GCL, Microquanta, Qcells, Caelux, Tandem PV and SolarEdge (you can read more about the program in
our 2026 review
). Together, Perovskite Connect and Electronics RESHAPED brought 600 people from 34 countries to the Estrel.
A truly global audience
Perovskite Connect is a truly international event. Two thirds of the attendees came from Europe, but one in three traveled from further away: 29 came from North America, 15 from Asia, and the rest from Israel, Australia, New Zealand and Colombia - from 10 different countries outside Europe.
Perovskite Connect also drew a more international crowd than the rest of the event. It accounted for just over a quarter of the total attendance in Berlin, but 41% of all the US attendees came for Perovskite Connect, as did almost 40% of those from Japan.
Germany sent the largest group, followed by the US, the UK, France and Switzerland. In Asia, Japan led the way, followed by India, China and Korea.
The whole value chain in one room
What makes Perovskite Connect special is that it brings the entire perovskite industry together. Materials suppliers made up about a quarter of the attendees (26%), with companies such as Solstice Advanced Materials, Nano-C, Fujifilm, H.B. Fuller and Air Liquide. They were followed by equipment and metrology suppliers (23%), including Coatema, Singulus, Bühler, LPKF, SENTECH and LayTec. Research institutes and universities, from HZB and imec to CEA-Leti, TNO, ZSW and the US National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL), made up another 19%.
For exhibitors and sponsors, the most important number may be this one: one in four people at the event came from the companies that make perovskite cells and modules, or that will use them in their products. These included Oxford PV, Qcells, First Solar, Panasonic, Heliatek, CubicPV, Caelux and SolarEdge.
What attendees said
After the event we asked attendees, speakers and exhibitors what they thought, and the feedback was great. Here are some of our favorites:
"Thank you for a fantastic event. It was extremely useful for us as an early-stage start-up. The masterclass and talks were high quality and very practical, the HZB tour was a highlight, and the networking drinks led to several valuable new connections."
- Nathaniel Davis, TwoPhold
"The event was very well organized and a lot of interesting contributions were given."
- Immo Koetschau, Oxford PV
Join us in 2027
Perovskite Connect 2027
will take place on October 20-21, 2027 at the Estrel Convention Center in Berlin, with masterclasses and tours on October 19. It will again be co-located with TechBlick's Future of Electronics RESHAPED. We expect the event to keep growing, as tandem production lines come online and more perovskite companies move from pilot lines to products. There are several ways to take part:
Exhibit or sponsor

: present your technology and roadmap to an expert audience from every part of the industry.
: meet the industry's key players in two days, at an event that is small enough to actually talk to them.
If you would like to exhibit, sponsor or present in 2027, please
contact us now

. See you in Berlin!

title: Nanodiamond reinforcement stabilizes soft perovskite lattice, enabling cells above 27% efficiency
content:
Nanodiamond reinforcement stabilizes soft perovskite lattice, enabling cells above 27% efficiency
Researchers at Zhejiang University, the ZJU-Hangzhou Global Scientific and Technological Innovation Center and the Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute in Beijing have stabilized perovskite solar cells by adding nanodiamonds that reinforce the boundaries between grains. Cells with the additive reached a certified efficiency above 27%, and minimodules reached 24.3%.
The team focused on the soft ionic lattice of halide perovskites, which expands and contracts as light and temperature change through day-night cycles. In polycrystalline films, grain boundaries are less constrained than grain interiors, so strain concentrates there. According to the researchers, this promotes ion migration and defect formation, which in turn distort the lattice further and make later cycles more damaging. Their measurements, including in situ nanoindentation and local creep tests, showed grain interiors deforming through dislocation-mediated creep and grain boundaries through intergranular sliding.
Inspired by ceramic-matrix composites, in which particles reinforce a brittle matrix, the team added nanodiamonds of about 10 nm to a formamidinium-cesium perovskite. The particles sit mainly in the intergranular regions. They suppress sliding and bring the boundary response closer to that of the grain interiors, making the films stiffer and more uniform. Simulations showed a more even stress distribution, and diffraction measurements showed reduced microstrain.
The reinforced films deformed less under temperature and illumination cycles. They also showed weaker electron-phonon coupling, fewer trap states, less non-radiative recombination and better charge extraction, which gave higher open-circuit voltage and fill factor. Small-area cells (0.09 cm²) reached a certified efficiency above 27%, and 16.1 cm² minimodules reached 24.3%.
In stability tests, devices kept 80% of their initial efficiency after 5,000 hours of maximum power point operation at 85 °C. They kept 98% after 5,000 hours of day-night cycling with varying light intensity. After aging, the reinforced films kept a compact morphology, with smaller increases in trap populations and mobile-ion density than the pristine perovskite.
The authors describe mechanical heterogeneity between grain interiors and boundaries as an important origin of perovskite instability, and present the reinforcement as a mechanical design principle for durable cells.

title: Offshore wind turbines used to restart power grid in blackout test
content:
Offshore wind turbines used to restart power grid in blackout test TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Offshore wind turbines used to restart power grid in blackout test
Energinet has announced the successful completion of tests in collaboration
with Vattenfall, 50Hertz and EnBW in which offshore wind turbines were
used to help restart the electricity grid following a simulated blackout
on Zealand. The companies said the trial is believed to be the first of
its kind.
According to Energinet, the test was designed to address a growing challenge
as renewable energy accounts for a larger share of power generation. Traditionally,
conventional power plants have been used to restore electricity grids after
major outages because they can provide a stable and controlled restart
process.
Renewable energy sources can be more variable due to weather conditions
and other external factors. As a result, grid operators are working to
ensure wind and solar power can also support system restoration during
major disruptions.
Under the test scenario, power was first restored through the connection
to Germany before electricity from the Kriegers Flak wind farm was gradually
fed into the grid. The turbines were then brought online one at a time,
allowing them to steadily contribute additional power as the restoration
process progressed.
“We must both work to avoid major power outages and be ready to restore
power if they do occur. With this test, we have shown that both the connection
to Germany and renewable energy from offshore wind can play an important
role,” said Klaus Winther, deputy director and head of system operations
at Energinet.
The successful trial demonstrates how offshore wind could play an increasingly
important role in grid restoration as renewable energy continues to replace
conventional generation sources.

title: AI Stocks’ Big Worry: a Chip Glut

That’s perhaps a sign that there are some things more important to the market than the fate of any one man, even our “geniuses,” as President Trump calls Huang. Worries that we could be headed for a glut of chips have percolated on Wall Street for months, without much evidence of such a surplus. title: In Private Funding, Like IPOs, Big Companies Dominate
content: Shares of Anthropic fell below its $83 IPO price on Tuesday morning, summing up what has been a tough year for IPOs. While a couple of monster IPOs got done—Anthropic and SpaceX—only a handful of others made it through including offerings from SK Hynix, Cerebras and Lime. And as of Tuesday, all of those were trading below their IPO price. That makes it the fifth year in a row when the IPO market has been at least a bit disappointing. A bunch of companies are lined up for next year—including OpenAI—but slumping tech valuations fueled by skepticism about the AI boom clouds prospects for 2027. In that context, it’s a decent time to take the pulse of startup dealmaking. One thing is clear: as in the IPO market this year, in the private fundraising market, the biggest companies are dominating. The top 10 private companies have more than doubled their combined valuation from $1.1 trillion to $2.6 trillion in just one year, Goldman’s top tech banker Jane Dunlevie said on stage last week at Goldman Sachs’ annual private tech conference in Las Vegas. She was talking about OpenAI, Anthropic, Databricks, Stripe, Waymo, Revolut, Anduril, Ramp, Cognition and Jeff Bezos's Prometheus. And more than half of those—OpenAI, Databricks, Anduril, Stripe, Ramp and Cognition—are now trying to raise billions more. There’s still plenty of smaller startups emerging. Goldman managed to play matchmaker for more than 400 investors and 400-plus startups in the gilded corridors at the Encore Wynn Hotel. The mood was still electric, though investors are starting to think: as public market valuations fall, how should we value these private companies? One reason why private valuations can stay elevated even as public stocks drop is that venture investors tend to zoom in on growth. Many of these AI businesses’ revenues have taken off, even as they bleed money thanks to expensive AI models they run and the chips they need to buy or rent. At a fireside chat at last week’s confab, Winston Weinberg, CEO of legal AI startup Harvey, acknowledged that even with fast revenue growth, its gross margins fell to about negative 55% around June. They improved the figure by about 95% in roughly three months. Weinberg said annualized revenue grew from $190 million at the end of last year and expected to end this year with at least $675 million. “We’re still early in the build out of AI, which means many of the defining companies of this era are not yet public and many investors are just getting to see the potential of those companies, both on growth and margin.” Goldman’s Jane Dunlevie said in an interview on the sidelines. She said each tech era has its own tests with investors: for internet companies, it was a path to profit; for subscription software firms, it was predictable revenue and net revenue retention. Meanwhile, attendees at the conference were staying hopeful about next year’s IPO market. Some predicted that older venture-backed startups, such as Vercel, Ramp and Plaid, and even the older vertical software companies with some AI makeover, such as AlphaSense and Clio, will finally go public. In the two days of investors’ schmoozing over fancy desserts and cocktails, a lineup of popular AI, chip and cybersecurity startups, like Legora, Unconventional AI and Abnormal AI fielded dozens of investors’ meeting requests. Many older software startups were trying to remind investors they still exist. They are not getting too much love, say bankers and investors. One barometer of who’s important in Las Vegas this year was whom Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon invited to his private dinner at the fancy restaurant Delilah. In attendance: Legora CEO Max Junestrand and Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao, said people familiar with the dinner. title: OpenAI Preps ‘Athena’ Data Tool to Make its Agents More Accurate
content: In its effort to win more business customers, OpenAI this fall launched an agent designed to help firms analyze their data and get answers to internal questions about their business. But at least one customer that has used the agent so far has found it isn’t yet accurate enough for widespread use. That’s a big problem. But OpenAI isn’t sitting still. Representatives of the ChatGPT creator have told some customers and partners that they are developing a data management platform to help the agent perform better, according to the customer and three other people who spoke to OpenAI in recent weeks. The data management platform, code-named Athena, has similarities to what is known in the industry as a semantic layer, which companies use to create standardized definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customers, one of the people said. This type of software helps agents understand the difference between gross revenue and net revenue, or active and paying customers, the person added. One of the biggest reasons agents fail when companies use them with large amounts of complex business data is that they have to work out on their own what the data means and how it fits together, said Jason Strimpel, a managing director at Andersen Consulting who helps large companies use AI. “A semantic layer gives the agent that context from the start, often with plain-English descriptions of each item, so the agent has to guess less and [can work] faster and more accurately,” he said.

title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
content:
AI is straining America’s open records systems
Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.
In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.
Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”
Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.
At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.
As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized
The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.
This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”
Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.
SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.
The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.
Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”
While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.
But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.
The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.
In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.
In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem
It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.
In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.
While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.
On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”
As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table
Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.
Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”
Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.
Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.
Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.
As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

Quirin Meyer weist den Weg: Grafikkarten sollen Geometrie nicht mehr speichern, sondern selbst erzeugen.
| Quelle:

Download
Wie bekommen Videospiele mehr Details auf den Bildschirm, wenn Arbeitsspeicher knapp und teuer wird? Diese Frage stand im Mittelpunkt der Keynote, mit der Prof. Dr. Quirin Meyer von der Hochschule Coburg am 17. November die Graphics Programming Conference (GPC) im niederländischen Breda eröffnete. Vor einem internationalen Fachpublikum aus der Spiele- und Grafikbranche zeigte er, wie Coburger Forschung Grafikkarten dazu bringt, Geometrie nicht mehr zu speichern, sondern bei Bedarf selbst zu erzeugen.
Dienstagmorgen, 9:15 Uhr, im großen Saal von „The Dock“ in Breda: Die Graphics Programming Conference beginnt, und als erster Redner steht ein Professor aus Coburg auf der Bühne. In den folgenden drei Tagen präsentierten Entwicklerinnen und Entwickler von NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Microsoft, Unity, Electronic Arts, Ubisoft, Remedy Entertainment, Keen Games, Wētā FX, Qualcomm, Arm, Adobe und zahlreichen weiteren Studios ihre neuesten Verfahren. Aus der Wissenschaft trugen neben Meyer auch Forschende der Yale University, der Breda University of Applied Sciences, des KTH Royal Institute of Technology und der Aalto University vor. Außerdem waren Apple, Huawei, die Blender Foundation und weitere Unternehmen vor Ort.
Rechenleistung wächst, Speicher nicht
„Grafikkarten rechnen seit Jahrzehnten immer schneller“, erklärt Meyer. „Daten zu bewegen und zu speichern hat damit nicht Schritt gehalten.“ Hinzu kommt eine aktuelle Entwicklung: Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz kaufen große Teile der weltweiten Produktion von Arbeitsspeicher und Festplatten auf.
Meyers Antwort auf diese Entwicklung lautet: weniger speichern, mehr berechnen. Statt riesige Mengen an Geometriedaten abzulegen und über den Speicherbus zu schicken, sollen Grafikkarten Details komprimiert vorhalten oder direkt dort erzeugen, wo sie gebraucht werden. „Die Rechenleistung ist da“, sagt Meyer. „Wir müssen nur lernen, sie klug einzusetzen.“
Eine einfache Idee, die sich durchgesetzt hat
Wie lange gute Ideen manchmal brauchen, zeigte Meyer an seiner eigenen Forschung. Bereits als Doktorand entwickelte er eine Methode, um Normalenvektoren, die für die Beleuchtung jedes Bildpunkts wichtig sind, mit rund der Hälfte des Speichers abzulegen, bei gleicher Genauigkeit. Die Arbeit wurde 2010 auf dem Eurographics Symposium on Rendering veröffentlicht. Heute findet sich die Idee in den Engines Unity und Godot, in Googles Kompressionsbibliothek Draco und in einer Erweiterung des Industriestandards glTF.
Eine zweite Arbeit aus Meyers Promotion zeigte, wie sich die Dreiecksstruktur von 3D-Modellen parallel auf der Grafikkarte entpacken lässt. Gemeinsam mit seinem Team und Partnern bei AMD hat Meyer diese Ideen seitdem weiterentwickelt, zuletzt für AMDs neues Geometrieformat „Dense Geometry Format“.
Wälder, die erst beim Hinsehen entstehen
Im zweiten Teil der Keynote zeigte Meyer, was möglich wird, wenn Grafikkarten Geometrie selbst erzeugen. Zusammen mit dem Industriepartner AMD lässt sein Team ganze Wälder mit individuellen Bäumen in Echtzeit auf der GPU wachsen, und zwar nur dort und nur so detailliert, wie es die Kamera gerade verlangt. In einem Beispiel aus der Keynote benötigt eine Vegetationsszene in einer klassischen Engine 35 Gigabyte vorab gespeicherter Geometrie. Das Verfahren kommt mit 51 Kilobyte Programmcode und 1,5 Gigabyte Zwischenspeicher aus, in dem die Grafikkarte die Bäume zur Laufzeit erzeugt.
Ein weiteres Projekt unterteilt gekrümmte Flächen, wie man sie aus der Fahrzeugkonstruktion kennt, adaptiv und lückenlos direkt auf der Grafikkarte. Die Arbeit entstand aus der Bachelorarbeit von Seyedmasih Tabaei und wurde 2026 auf dem Eurographics Symposium on Rendering veröffentlicht.
Am Ende richtete Meyer einen Appell an beide Seiten: Forschende sollten ihren Quellcode veröffentlichen und auf die Industrie zugehen, Unternehmen in Forschung investieren und ihre Probleme mit Hochschulen teilen. „Gute Ideen setzen sich nicht von allein durch“, sagt Meyer. „Sie müssen auch dort ankommen, wo Software tatsächlich entsteht.“
Forschung mit internationaler Sichtbarkeit
Die Coburger Arbeitsgruppe forscht seit Jahren eng mit dem Grafikkartenhersteller AMD zusammen und wurde mehrfach mit Best-Paper-Awards ausgezeichnet. Im Projekt SimuFlow untersucht sie gemeinsam mit AMD bis 2029, wie Grafikkarten Geometrie, Beleuchtung und Physiksimulationen effizienter berechnen können. Die Bayerische Transformations- und Forschungsstiftung fördert das Vorhaben mit rund 430.000 Euro.
Die GPC wurde 2024 von den Branchenveteranen Johan Andersson, Jasper Bekkers und Matthäus Chajdas gegründet und hat sich schnell zu einem Treffpunkt der europäischen Grafik-Community entwickelt. Neben Meyer hielt Chas. Boyd, Senior Fellow bei AMD, die zweite Keynote der Konferenz. In insgesamt 39 Vorträgen ging es unter anderem um die Grafik aktueller Spiele wie „007 First Light“, „Helldivers 2“, „Subnautica 2“, „No Man’s Sky“, „Enshrouded“ und „Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced“.
Für Studierende der Hochschule Coburg ist das Thema nah am Studium: Meyer leitet den Bachelorstudiengang Visual Computing, in dem Computergrafik, Bildverarbeitung und Künstliche Intelligenz im Mittelpunkt stehen. „Wer heute KI und Grafik programmiert, muss Hardware verstehen“, sagt Meyer. „Genau das lernen unsere Studierenden, und einige von ihnen veröffentlichen ihre Ergebnisse bereits während des Studiums auf internationalen Konferenzen.“

title: Bürgerrat zu Drohnenverkehr nimmt Arbeit auf
content:
Bürgerrat zu Drohnenverkehr nimmt Arbeit auf
Bis Februar 2027 werden 100 zufällig, aber repräsentativ ausgewählte Bürger*innen Empfehlungen zum Drohnen-Lieferverkehr erarbeiten – Start am 27. November 2026 in Potsdam
Mit der Weiterentwicklung der Drohnentechnologie eröffnen sich für den Lieferverkehr völlig neue Möglichkeiten. Doch wie genau soll der städtische und ländliche Luftraum in Zukunft genutzt werden? Darüber werden sich ab dem 27. November 100 Bürger*innen beraten, Expert*innen anhören und schließlich Empfehlungen abgeben. Dabei spielen Ideen für neue Geschäftsmodelle, Infrastrukturen und Dienstleistungen genauso eine Rolle wie Fragen nach Sicherheit, Geräuschemissionen und gesellschaftlichen Auswirkungen. Die Empfehlungen sollen der Politik Anhaltspunkte dafür liefern, welche Anwendungen des Lieferverkehrs mit Drohnen aus Sicht von Bürger*innen als nützlich erachtet werden und wo reguliert werden muss, um unerwünschte Folgen zu vermeiden. Realisiert wird das Projekt von der Forschungsgruppe ELEVATE am Fachgebiet Arbeitslehre/Technik und Partizipation (ArTe) der TU Berlin mit Beteiligung des nexus Instituts für Kooperationsmanagement und interdisziplinäre Forschung.
Der unbemannte Lieferverkehr ist eines der Schlüsseltechnologiefelder der Deutschen Hightech-Agenda. Eine herausragende Rolle spielt dabei die Drohnentechnologie. „Dies erfordert ein völliges Umdenken. Statt in Quadratmetern muss die Stadtplanung künftig in Kubikmetern rechnen“, erklärt Projektleiter Dr. Robin Kellermann vom Fachgebiet ArTe der TU Berlin. Bisher würden die Auswirkungen einer verstärkten Nutzung unseres Luftraums aber kaum diskutiert.
„Die Einführung der Technologie steht allerdings auch ganz am Anfang, so dass wir noch Zeit haben, mit klugen Entscheidungen die Entwicklungen in die richtigen Bahnen zu lenken.“ Genau hier setzt die Forschungsgruppe ELEVATE an, die von Kellermann geleitet und vom Bundesforschungsministerium im Rahmen seiner FONA-Strategie (Forschung für Nachhaltigkeit) mit vier Millionen Euro über fünf Jahre gefördert wird. Der Bürgerrat ist eines der Projekte der Forschungsgruppe.
Regulierung des unteren Luftraums bezieht künftige Nutzungsmöglichkeiten bisher nicht ein
In einem Zeitraum von gut zwei Monaten werden sich 100 Bürger*innen mit dem Drohnen-Lieferverkehr beschäftigen: Sie recherchieren, diskutieren, hören Expert*innen an und beschließen am Ende Empfehlungen, die der Politik übergeben werden – unter anderem der Berliner Senatsverwaltung für Mobilität, Verkehr, Klimaschutz und Umwelt.
„Lieferdrohnen bieten rein technisch betrachtet Möglichkeiten für eine verbesserte Erreichbarkeit und effizientere Logistik. Zugleich muss man diskutieren, wofür und unter welchen Bedingungen eine Lieferung aus der Luft überhaupt gesellschaftlich sinnvoll und akzeptabel erscheint“, sagt Kellermann. „Eine unabhängige Beurteilung durch eine repräsentative Gruppe der Bevölkerung in Berlin und Brandenburg ist hier für die Politik also sehr hilfreich.“ Zudem hätten die Empfehlungen nicht nur für die Landes-, sondern auch für die Bundespolitik Bedeutung, da die meisten Regelungen bezüglich unseres Luftraums Bundesgesetze sind.
Repräsentative Zusammensetzung der Teilnehmenden aus Berlin und Brandenburg
„Am Format der Bürgerräte als Teil der demokratischen Willensbildung wird häufig kritisiert, dass sich hier nur ein engagierter Ausschnitt der Bevölkerung einbringen würde und die dort beschlossenen Empfehlungen damit nicht repräsentativ seien“, sagt Volkan Sayman vom nexus Institut, das den Bürgerrat gemeinsam mit dem Fachgebiet ArTe umsetzt. „Wir haben großen Wert darauf gelegt, die Teilnehmenden durch eine methodisch saubere Zufallsauswahl zu ermitteln. Aus dem Pool der zufällig ausgewählten und zur Teilnahme bereiten Personen haben wir dann die Teilnehmenden so selektiert, dass wir eine für Berlin und Brandenburg repräsentative Zusammensetzung erhalten.“
Angeschrieben wurden 7.000 zufällig ausgewählte Personen in Berlin und Brandenburg, von denen sich 250 für eine Teilnahme interessierten. Aus dieser Menge haben die Forschenden dann 100 Menschen ausgewählt, um eine nach Alter, Geschlecht, Bildungsstand, Wohnortgröße und weiteren Faktoren repräsentativ zusammengesetzte Gruppe zu bilden.
„Die Hälfte der Teilnehmenden stammt aus Brandenburg, die andere aus Berlin. Wir haben Menschen aus kleinen Dörfern mit dabei, aus Klein- und Großstädten. Wir möchten gerne alle Bürger*innen einbeziehen und stellen daher Unterstützungsangebote zur Verfügung. Daher sind Menschen mit kognitiven Einschränkungen ebenso vertreten wie Personen, die nicht gut Deutsch sprechen und eine Übersetzung brauchen. Auch Personen, die eine Kinderbetreuung benötigen, können ebenfalls teilnehmen“, so Sayman.
Technologische Innovationen bei der zivilen Anwendung von Drohnen sind zu erwarten
Bereits im Vorfeld des nun startenden Bürgerrats haben die Forschenden durch Befragung von Expert*innen und Gespräche mit Fokusgruppen fünf Themenfelder identifiziert, die für die Menschen in Berlin und Brandenburg von besonderem Interesse sind: die mögliche Lärmbelastung, die durchdachte Planung von Flugrouten, Fragen des Datenschutzes, sinnvolle neue Anwendungsfelder von Drohnen sowie sowohl positive als auch negative soziale, wirtschaftliche und ökologische Folgen. „Nicht nur in der Stadt, sondern gerade auch auf dem Land könnten Drohnen, die zwei bis fünf Kilogramm Fracht über bis zu 80 Kilometer weit tragen können, die Versorgung der Bevölkerung verbessern. Und weitere technische Innovationen sind zu erwarten, denn zivile Einsatzbereiche werden von den technologischen Fortschritten profitieren, die momentan leider vor allem durch militärische Anwendungen vorangetrieben werden“, erklärt Robin Kellermann vom Fachgebiet ArTe.
Start am 27. November 2026 – Öffentliche Übergabe der Empfehlungen am 13. Februar 2027
Die Auftaktveranstaltung des Bürgerrats zum Drohnenverkehr findet am 27. und 28. November 2027 in Präsenz im Tagungsort „Langer Stall“ im Potsdamer Kreativ-Quartier statt. Hier besteht für Pressevertreter*innen die Möglichkeit, am Beginn der Veranstaltung um 16:00 Uhr teilzunehmen. Eine Anwesenheit während der inhaltlichen Diskussionen und Arbeiten ist nicht vorgesehen. Nach mehreren digitalen Sitzungen im Dezember und Januar werden die Empfehlungen des Bürgerrats am 13. Februar 2027 ebenfalls im Langen Stall in Potsdam der Öffentlichkeit vorgestellt und politischen Vertreter*innen offiziell übergeben. Hierzu folgt eine gesonderte Einladung.
„Damit ist unsere Arbeit an diesem Projekt aber noch lange nicht zu Ende“, sagt Robin Kellermann. In einer Begleitforschung werden sowohl der konkrete Umgang der Politik mit den – nicht bindenden – Empfehlungen wie auch die möglichen Nachwirkungen auf die Teilnehmenden des Bürgerrats durch die Forschungsgruppe ELEVATE untersucht. Zudem realisiert ELEVATE ab Mitte 2027 zwei Reallabore in Brandenburg und Berlin, um die Potenziale und Grenzen des Einsatzes von Lieferdrohnen konkret mess- und erfahrbar machen zu können.
